be feared that his house and his position in society, and the prospect
of unlimited millinery, were more to her than Mr Cavendish. All these
details were not perhaps contemplated by himself as he devoted himself
to the handsome contralto.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Penetrating analysis of Barbara's true motivations: social advancement and material comfort rather than genuine love; reveals the hollowness of her passion through ironic observation.

enrichment.summary: Barbara's motivations are primarily mercenary: his house, social position, and unlimited millinery matter more to her than Mr Cavendish himself.

text:
He had not begun to dream, as Barbara had
done for a long time, of the wedding breakfast and the orange blossoms,
or even of furnishing a new drawing-room handsomer than Miss
Marjoribanks's, and giving parties which should be real parties and not
mere Thursdays. None of these imaginations occupied Mr Cavendish as he
followed Barbara's glowing cheeks and flashing eyes to his undoing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Contrasts Mr Cavendish's lack of serious matrimonial intention with Barbara's elaborate dreams; explains the mismatch between their motivations but remains expository.
enrichment.best_quote: He had not begun to dream, as Barbara had done for a long time, of the wedding breakfast and the orange blossoms, or even of furnishing a new drawing-room handsomer than Miss Marjoribanks's
enrichment.summary: Mr Cavendish has not contemplated marriage or household furnishing as Barbara has; he is drawn purely by her beauty and charm.

text:
But
then if he did not mean it she meant it; and, after all, there are
occasions in which the woman's determination is the more important of
the two. So that, taking everything into consideration, there can be no
doubt that it was very fortunate that Lucilla's affections were not
engaged. She behaved as nobody else in Carlingford was capable of
behaving, and very few people anywhere, according to Mrs Chiley's
admiring belief.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Pronounces Barbara's determination more important than Mr Cavendish's intentions, making his disengagement impossible; argues Lucilla's unengaged affections were fortunate and her behaviour superior to all others.
enrichment.best_quote: there are occasions in which the woman's determination is the more important of the two
enrichment.summary: The narrator asserts that Barbara's determination is more powerful than Mr Cavendish's intentions, making it very fortunate that Lucilla's affections were not engaged.

text:
It was not for a vulgar antagonist like Barbara Lake to
touch Lucilla. The way in which she asked her to lunch and went on
practising duets with her was angelical—it brought the tears to Mrs
Chiley's eyes; and as for the domestic traitor whom Miss Marjoribanks
thus contrived to warm in her magnanimous bosom, she was sometimes so
full of spite and disappointment that she could neither eat her lunch
nor go on with her singing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Describes Lucilla's magnanimous treatment of Barbara through invitations and duets, which moves Mrs Chiley to tears but torments Barbara with incomplete triumph; reveals the dynamics of power and spite.
enrichment.best_quote: The way in which she asked her to lunch and went on practising duets with her was angelical—it brought the tears to Mrs Chiley's eyes
enrichment.summary: Lucilla magnanimously invites Barbara to lunch and continues their musical duets, moving Mrs Chiley to tears while tormenting Barbara with her serene unconsciousness.

text:
For, to be sure, the dearest climax of her
triumph was wanting so long as Lucilla took no notice; and so far from
taking any notice, Miss Marjoribanks was sweeter and more friendly than
usual in her serene unconsciousness. "I am so afraid you have caught
cold," Lucilla would say; "if you don't feel clear in your lower notes,
we can pass over this passage, you know, for to-day.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's perfectly solicitous remarks to Barbara about her health and vocal condition demonstrate exquisite psychological torture through false concern; reveals the cruelty beneath magnanimity.
enrichment.best_quote: I am so afraid you have caught cold; if you don't feel clear in your lower notes, we can pass over this passage, you know, for to-day
enrichment.summary: Lucilla expresses solicitous concern for Barbara's health and vocal condition with perfect courtesy, suggesting she defer challenging passages.

text:
You must see papa
before you go away, and he will order you something; but, my dear
Barbara, you must take care." And then Barbara could have eaten her
fingers instead of the gloves which she kept biting in her vexation. For, to tell the truth, if Miss Marjoribanks was not jealous, the
victory was but half a victory after all.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Final revelation that Barbara's triumph requires Lucilla's acknowledgement; without jealousy from Lucilla, victory is hollow—Lucilla's magnanimity denies Barbara the satisfaction of causing pain.
enrichment.best_quote: if Miss Marjoribanks was not jealous, the victory was but half a victory after all
enrichment.summary: Barbara's ultimate frustration is that without Lucilla's jealousy, her victory is incomplete; Lucilla's magnanimous indifference denies her the validation of triumph.

text:
It was thus that Miss Marjoribanks went through all the preliminary
stages, and succeeded finally in making a triumph out of what would
certainly have been a defeat, and a humbling defeat, for anybody else.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the chapter's central achievement but in abstract, summarising terms that lack concrete detail.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla converts what could have been a humiliating defeat into a triumph.

text:
She was much too sensible to deceive herself on the subject, or not to
be aware that to have a gentleman who was paying attention to her
withdrawn from her side in this open manner in the sight of all the
world, was as trying an accident as can happen to a woman. Fortunately,
as Lucilla said, her affections were not engaged; but then, apart from
the affections, there are other sentiments which demand consideration.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the psychological stakes of public romantic rejection, but the analysis is somewhat didactic rather than dramatically rendered.
enrichment.best_quote: her affections were not engaged; but then, apart from the affections, there are other sentiments which demand consideration
enrichment.summary: Lucilla recognises that losing a gentleman's attentions in public is damaging beyond mere affection.

text:
Everybody in Carlingford knew that Mr Cavendish had been paying her a
great deal of attention, and the situation was one which required the
most delicate skill to get through it successfully. Besides, Miss
Marjoribanks's circumstances were all the more difficult, since up to
this moment she had been perfectly sincere and natural in all her
proceedings.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Provides necessary exposition about Carlingford's knowledge of the situation but remains procedural rather than engaging.
enrichment.summary: Carlingford is aware of Mr Cavendish's attentions to Lucilla, making her situation delicate and requiring careful management.

text:
Policy had been constantly inspired and backed by nature in
the measures Lucilla had taken for the organisation and welfare of her
kingdom, and even what people took for the cleverest calculation was in
reality a succession of happy instincts, by means of which, with the
sovereignty of true genius, Miss Marjoribanks managed to please
everybody by having her own way.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Offers keen psychological insight into Lucilla's character, suggesting that her calculation masks genuine instinct and genius.
enrichment.best_quote: Policy had been constantly inspired and backed by nature in the measures Lucilla had taken for the organisation and welfare of her kingdom
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's success derives not from cold calculation but from happy instincts and true genius that blend policy with natural feeling.

text:
A little victory is almost necessary to
begin with, and it is a poor nature that does not expand under the
stimulus of victory; but now the young reformer had come to the second
stage. For, to be sure, that sort of thing cannot last for ever; and
this Lucilla, with the natural prevision of a ruling mind, had foreseen
from the beginning.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Moves into abstract discussion of Lucilla's strategic foresight, but lacks dramatic specificity.
enrichment.best_quote: A little victory is almost necessary to begin with, and it is a poor nature that does not expand under the stimulus of victory
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has moved beyond early victories into a second stage, having foreseen from the start that success cannot last indefinitely.

text:
The shape in which she had feared defeat, if a
nature so full of resources could ever be said to fear, was that of a
breakdown, when all the world was looking to her for amusement, or the
sudden appearance of a rival entertainer in Carlingford with superior
powers: though the last was but a dim and improbable danger, the first
was quite possible, and might have arrived at any moment.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Identifies potential threats to Lucilla's dominance, but treats them speculatively rather than with concrete drama.
enrichment.best_quote: a breakdown, when all the world was looking to her for amusement, or the sudden appearance of a rival entertainer in Carlingford with superior powers
enrichment.summary: Lucilla had anticipated two possible defeats: a social collapse during a Thursday event or the arrival of a superior rival entertainer.

text:
Miss
Marjoribanks was much too sensible not to have foreseen this danger in
all its shapes, and even in a kind of way to have provided against it. But Providence, which had always taken care of her, as Lucilla piously
concluded, had spared her the trial in that form.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Asserts Lucilla's foresight and reliance on providence, but offers little new content or engagement.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has sensibly anticipated dangers and taken precautions, though she credits Providence for protecting her.

text:
Up to this moment it
had always providentially happened that all the principal people in
Carlingford were quite well and disengaged on the "evening." To be sure,
the ladies had headaches, and the married gentlemen now and then were
out of temper in Grange Lane as in other less favoured places; but these
social accidents had been mercifully averted on Thursdays, perhaps by
means of some special celestial agency, perhaps only through that
good-luck which had been born with Lucilla.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uses gentle irony to describe social synchronicity, with some amusing detail about Thursday gatherings.
enrichment.best_quote: all the principal people in Carlingford were quite well and disengaged on the "evening"
enrichment.summary: Until now, Thursday events have been providentially blessed with full attendance and good health, despite minor domestic ailments elsewhere.

text:
Not in this vulgar and
likely manner was the trial of her strength to come.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief transitional assertion that provides no new information or rhetorical force.
enrichment.summary: The trial Lucilla faces will not be of this mundane sort.

text:
But when she was at the height of her success, and full in the eye of
the world, and knew that everybody was remarking her, and that from the
sauces for which the Doctor's table was once so famed, but which even
Colonel Chiley no longer thought of identifying as Dr Marjoribanks's, to
the fashion of the  high  white frock in which Lucilla had taught the
young ladies of Carlingford to appear of an evening, she was being
imitated on every hand,—at that moment, when an ordinary person would
have had her head turned, and gone wild with too much success, Miss
Marjoribanks suddenly saw her dragon approaching her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid and dramatic description of Lucilla's dominance of Carlingford society at the moment of crisis, with wonderful accumulated detail and a powerful metaphorical turn at the close.
enrichment.best_quote: at that moment, when an ordinary person would have had her head turned, and gone wild with too much success, Miss Marjoribanks suddenly saw her dragon approaching her
enrichment.summary: At the height of her social triumph, when all Carlingford imitates her in dress, manners, and cuisine, Lucilla suddenly perceives danger approaching.

text:
Just then, when
she could not put on a new ribbon, or do her hair in a different style,
without all Carlingford knowing of it—at that epoch of intoxication and
triumph the danger came, sudden, appalling, and unlooked for. If Lucilla
was staggered by the encounter, she never showed it, but met the
difficulty like a woman of mettle, and scorned to flinch.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Heightens tension by emphasising the public scrutiny and suddenness of the crisis, while characterising Lucilla's stoic response.
enrichment.best_quote: at that epoch of intoxication and triumph the danger came, sudden, appalling, and unlooked for
enrichment.summary: The crisis arrives without warning during Lucilla's moment of greatest prominence and public observation, yet she meets it without flinching.

text:
It had come to
be summer weather when the final day arrived upon which Mr Cavendish
forgot himself altogether, and went over to the insidious enemy whom
Miss Marjoribanks had been nourishing in her bosom. Fifty eyes were upon
Lucilla watching her conduct at that critical moment—fifty ears were on
the strain to divine her sentiments in her voice, and to catch some
intonation at least which should betray her consciousness of what was
going on.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dramatically captures the moment of Mr Cavendish's public defection to Barbara Lake, with intense focus on the watching crowd and Lucilla's composure under scrutiny.
enrichment.best_quote: Fifty eyes were upon Lucilla watching her conduct at that critical moment—fifty ears were on the strain to divine her sentiments in her voice
enrichment.summary: Mr Cavendish openly abandons Lucilla for Barbara Lake in summer weather, with the entire community watching to gauge Lucilla's emotional response.

text:
But if Miss Marjoribanks's biographer has fitly discharged his duty, the
readers of this history will have no difficulty in divining that the
curiosity of the spectators got no satisfaction from Lucilla. Many
people even supposed she had not remarked anything, her composure was so
perfect.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A meta-narrative aside claiming Lucilla maintained composure so perfect that many did not even notice her awareness, but the observation is somewhat arch.
enrichment.best_quote: the curiosity of the spectators got no satisfaction from Lucilla
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's composure was so complete that some spectators believed she had not even noticed the betrayal.

text:
No growing red or growing pale, no harsh notes in her voice,
nor evidence of distracted attention, betrayed that her mind was
elsewhere while she was attending to her guests; and yet, to be sure,
she saw, just as other people did, that Barbara, all flushed and
crimson, with her eyes blazing under their sullen brows, stood in a glow
of triumph at the open window, with Mr Cavendish in devoted
attendance—a captive at her chariot-wheels.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Describes Lucilla's outward composure while acknowledging her inward awareness, creating ironic tension and vivid detail of Barbara's triumph.
enrichment.best_quote: Barbara, all flushed and crimson, with her eyes blazing under their sullen brows, stood in a glow of triumph at the open window, with Mr Cavendish in devoted attendance—a captive at her chariot-wheels
enrichment.summary: While maintaining perfect composure, Lucilla observes Barbara flushed with triumph and Mr Cavendish in devoted attendance at the window.

text:
Matters had been
progressing to this point for some time; but yet the two culprits had
never before showed themselves so lost to all sense of propriety. Instead of fainting or getting pale, or showing any other symptoms of
violent despite, Lucilla went upon her airy way, indirectly approaching
this point of interest. She went up and chatted with them, and ordered
Mr Cavendish to find a chair for Barbara.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shows Lucilla's masterful response in real time—addressing the situation indirectly with consummate skill that humiliates the culprits.
enrichment.best_quote: Instead of fainting or getting pale, or showing any other symptoms of violent despite, Lucilla went upon her airy way, indirectly approaching this point of interest
enrichment.summary: Rather than betray emotion, Lucilla coolly addresses the situation by chatting with the couple and insisting Barbara sit safely away from the window.

text:
"What can you be thinking of
to let her stand so near the window? If she were to catch cold and lose
her voice, what should we all do?" said Lucilla; and she established the
two in the most commodious corner before she left them. "Take care she
does not go back again into the draught," were her parting words, and
even the culprits themselves could do nothing but stare at each other
with consternation and shame.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's final taunt masked as concern for Barbara's health is devastating and quotable, leaving the culprits mortified.
enrichment.best_quote: What can you be thinking of to let her stand so near the window? If she were to catch cold and lose her voice, what should we all do?
enrichment.summary: Lucilla settles the couple comfortably, then departs with a pointed reminder that Barbara should not return to the draught, leaving them in consternation.

text:
This was all the notice Lucilla took of what was going on. If she was
affronted, or if she was wounded, nobody found it out; and when Mrs
Chiley offered the tribute of her indignation and sympathy, it has
already been recorded how her young friend responded to her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Summary assertion that Lucilla revealed no wound, with a forward reference to Mrs Chiley's response already recorded.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla showed no sign of being wounded, and when Mrs Chiley offered sympathy, Lucilla responded appropriately.

text:
"Fortunately my affections never were engaged," Lucilla said, and no
doubt that was a great advantage; but then, as we have said, there are
other things besides affections to be taken into account when the woman
whom you have been kind to snaps up the man who has been paying
attention to you, not only before your eyes, but before the eyes of all
the world.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reiterates Lucilla's claim that affections were not engaged, but uses it to explore broader social injury beyond romantic feeling.
enrichment.best_quote: there are other things besides affections to be taken into account when the woman whom you have been kind to snaps up the man who has been paying attention to you, not only before your eyes, but before the eyes of all the world
enrichment.summary: While Lucilla maintains her affections were not engaged, the narrator reflects on other sentiments at stake when a protégée steals a suitor publicly.

text:
The result of her masterly conduct on this occasion was that
her defeat became, as we have said, a triumph for Miss Marjoribanks. To
be sure, it is to be hoped that, in the sweets of their mutual regard,
the two criminals found compensation for the disapproval of the
spectators; but nothing could be more marked than the way in which
Carlingford turned its cold shoulder on its early favourite.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shows the remarkable outcome: Lucilla's defeat becomes a triumph as Carlingford turns on both Cavendish and Barbara, vindicating her skill.
enrichment.best_quote: To be sure, it is to be hoped that, in the sweets of their mutual regard, the two criminals found compensation for the disapproval of the spectators; but nothing could be more marked than the way in which Carlingford turned its cold shoulder on its early favourite
enrichment.summary: Paradoxically, Lucilla's defeat becomes a triumph as Carlingford collectively withdraws favour from both Mr Cavendish and Barbara.

text:
"I never
imagined Cavendish was such a fool," Mr Centum said, who was a man of
few words; "if he likes that style of philandering, it is nothing to me,
but he need not make an idiot of himself." As for Mr Woodburn, he, as
was natural, inflicted vicarious punishment upon his wife.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shows the community's collective disapproval through two representative male voices, with some characterising detail but limited depth.
enrichment.best_quote: I never imagined Cavendish was such a fool
enrichment.summary: Mr Centum dismisses Cavendish as a fool, while Mr Woodburn prepares to blame his wife for failing to stop his folly.

"It must be
all your fault," he growled, when he was taking her home, and had her
at his mercy, with that logic peculiar to a married man; "you ought to
tell him he's making an ass of himself. Why the deuce do you let him go
on with that tomfoolery? He'll lose all his chances in life, and then, I

enrichment.interest_rationale: Captures Mr Woodburn's petulant blaming of his wife with some comic effect, showing how public scandal infects private relations.
enrichment.best_quote: It must be all your fault

text:
You women can never see an inch before your
own noses!" cried the uncivil husband; which, it must be confessed, was
rather hard upon poor Mrs Woodburn, who had nothing to do with it, and
had indeed calculated upon perfecting her sketch of Barbara in the
quietness of the walk home; for as everybody lived in Grange Lane,
carriages were not necessary for Miss Marjoribanks's guests.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uses domestic comedy to show Mr Woodburn's irrational venting while introducing a detail about the guests' walk home and Mrs Woodburn's artistic plans.
enrichment.best_quote: You women can never see an inch before your own noses!
enrichment.summary: Mr Woodburn continues his unreasonable tirade, while Mrs Woodburn had been planning to sketch Barbara on the return walk home.

They
flitted out and in, in the moonlight, with pretty scarfs thrown over
their heads and laced handkerchiefs tied under their chins, and made
Grange Lane between the two straight lines of garden-wall like a scene
in a masquerade.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Offers a brief, lyrical description of the guests departing through moonlit Grange Lane, creating a romantic scene before the darker revelations to come.

text:
While Mr Cavendish was thus suffering by deputy the contempt of his
former admirers, Lucilla, by herself in the abandoned drawing-room, was
thinking over the evening with a severe but on the whole satisfactory
self-examination. After the first shock, which she had encountered with
so much courage, Miss Marjoribanks was rather grateful than otherwise to
Providence, which had brought the necessary trial upon her in this form.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shifts to Lucilla's private reflection, showing her strategic satisfaction and gratitude that the trial came in a manageable form.
enrichment.best_quote: Lucilla, by herself in the abandoned drawing-room, was thinking over the evening with a severe but on the whole satisfactory self-examination

text:
If it had been a breakdown and humiliating failure instead, how
different would her sensations have been! and Lucilla was quite
conscious that such a thing might have occurred. It might have occurred
to her, as it had done to so many people, to see Thursday come round
with a failure of all that made Thursday agreeable.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Elaborates Lucilla's relief that the trial did not take the form of a complete social breakdown.
enrichment.best_quote: how different would her sensations have been!
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reflects that a breakdown during a Thursday evening would have been far more damaging than losing Mr Cavendish's attention.

text:
Lady Richmond might
have had her influenza that day, and little Henry Centum his sudden
attack, which had kept his mother in conversation ever since, and Mrs

text:
Or, to turn to another
chapter of accidents, the last duet, which Barbara had insisted upon
singing without proper practice, might have broken down utterly. None of
these things had happened, and Lucilla drew a long breath of gratitude
as she thought how fortunate she had been in all these particulars.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Notes that a musical failure might have undermined the evening, but the duet succeeded, confirming Lucilla's good fortune overall.
enrichment.summary: The final duet, which might have failed, instead succeeded, completing Lucilla's evening of preserved good fortune.

text:
To
be sure, it was necessary to have a trial of one kind or other; and the

enrichment.best_quote: the modest but intense gratification of having stood the test, diffused itself like a balm through her bosom
enrichment.summary: Lucilla finds deep satisfaction in having endured the trial with dignity and maintained her composure.

text:

most people, a certain pleasure in snubbing Barbara; but then there is,
on the other hand, a sweetness in sacrificing such impulses to the

the candles, and went to her own room with that feeling of having

While all this was going on, Dr Marjoribanks remained an amused
spectator, and chuckled a little quietly, without saying anything to
anybody, over the turn affairs had taken. The Doctor knew all about
everybody in Carlingford, and he had never been an enthusiast in favour

text:
Perhaps Dr
Marjoribanks being Scotch, and having a turn for genealogy, found the
description a little vague; but at all events there can be no doubt that
he laughed to himself as he retired from the scene of his daughter's
trial. The Doctor possibly thought, in a professional point of view,
that a little discipline of this description would be useful to Lucilla.

text:
Perhaps he thought it would be good for her to find out that—though she
had managed to slip the reins out of his hands, and get the control of
affairs with a skill which amused the Doctor, and made him a little
proud of her abilities, even though he was himself the victim—she could
not go on always unchecked in her triumphant career, but must endure
like other people an occasional defeat.

enrichment.summary: The Doctor hopes the events teach Lucilla that despite her skill in seizing power from him, she cannot triumph indefinitely without occasional setback.

text:
No doubt, had Lucilla been
really worsted, paternal feeling would have interposed, and Dr
Marjoribanks would to some extent have suffered in her suffering; but
then the case was different, and nobody required, as it turned out, to

affections had not been engaged; but there were more things than

 her  house who was not what he appeared to be? When such an idea

too hasty heed to anything, nor to put herself in the wrong by any

We have no wealth; but we
have some things which cannot be purchased by wealth," said the
drawing-master, with mild grandeur; and he looked round upon the walls
of his parlour, which were hung with his own drawings, and where one of
Willie's held the place of honour.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Lake's pride in his artistic accomplishments and his daughter's art is revealed, showing his values and the household's atmosphere.
enrichment.best_quote: We have no wealth; but we have some things which cannot be purchased by wealth
enrichment.summary: Mr Lake speaks of his family's lack of wealth while gesturing to his own drawings and his son Willie's artwork adorning the parlour walls.

text:
In all Carlingford there was no other
house that enjoyed a similar distinction; and, consequently, it was with
a delicious sense of chivalrous deference yet equality that the
exceptional man of Grove Street received the young sovereign of Grange
Lane.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Emphasizes the uniqueness of the Lakes' household and establishes the ironic dynamic between Mr Lake's pride and his modest status.
enrichment.summary: No other house in Carlingford displays art like Grove Street, so Mr Lake receives Lucilla with a blend of deference and equality.

text:
"I am so glad to come, Mr Lake," said Lucilla. "It is so nice to be
among such old friends; and, besides that, you know there never was any
voice that suited mine like Barbara's; and that dear old Rose was always
my pet at Mount Pleasant. I should have come long ago if anybody had
ever asked me," said Miss Marjoribanks.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla employs flattery and nostalgia to ingratiate herself, revealing her strategic social charm and implicit criticism of the Lakes.
enrichment.best_quote: you know there never was any voice that suited mine like Barbara's; and that dear old Rose was always my pet at Mount Pleasant
enrichment.summary: Lucilla praises the Lakes and claims she would have visited sooner had she been asked, subtly reproaching their lack of invitation.

text:
And as for Mr Lake, he was so
overpowered by this implied reproach upon his hospitality that he
scarcely knew how to reply.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Lake's anxious response is a routine social reaction to Lucilla's implied reproach.
enrichment.summary: Mr Lake is disturbed by Lucilla's implication that the Lakes have not invited her.

text:
"My dear Miss Marjoribanks, if you have not been asked it has been from
no want of—of goodwill," said Mr Lake anxiously. "I do not know what
the girls can have been thinking of. You see Rose's genius takes another
line; and Barbara, naturally, has a great many things to think of; but
in the future, I hope——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Lake's anxious defence of his daughters is a routine conversational moment without significant plot or thematic weight.
enrichment.summary: Mr Lake apologetically explains that Rose's genius and Barbara's many thoughts have prevented them from inviting Lucilla, but hopes to improve.

text:
"Oh, yes; I shall come without being asked," said Lucilla. And when the
tea came it was all she could do to keep herself quiet, and remember
that she was a visitor, and not take it out of the incapable hands of
Barbara, who never gave her father the right amount of sugar in his tea.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's remark about visiting without being asked, combined with her critical observation of Barbara's incompetence with tea, reveals her superior management sensibilities and class consciousness.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh, yes; I shall come without being asked
enrichment.summary: Lucilla declares she will visit without invitation, then silently criticizes Barbara's inability to properly serve tea to her father.

text:
To tell the truth, Barbara's thoughts were occupied by a very different
subject; and even Rose had but little attention to spare for her papa's
comforts at that special moment. But Lucilla's larger mind embraced
everything.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Contrasts Barbara's and Rose's distraction with Lucilla's comprehensive attention, establishing her superior consciousness and management abilities.
enrichment.best_quote: Lucilla's larger mind embraced everything
enrichment.summary: While Barbara and Rose are distracted by their own concerns, Lucilla's comprehensive mind attends to Mr Lake's comfort.

text:
She sat with her very fingers itching to cut the
bread-and-butter for him, and give him a cup of tea as he liked it; and
asked herself, with indignation, what was the use of that great
creature, with her level eyebrows and her crimson bloom, who could not
take the trouble to remember that three lumps was what Mr Lake liked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's internal indignation at Barbara's incompetence is vividly rendered, revealing her contempt for those who lack proper management skills.
enrichment.best_quote: She sat with her very fingers itching to cut the bread-and-butter for him, and give him a cup of tea as he liked it; and asked herself, with indignation, what was the use of that great creature, with her level eyebrows and her crimson bloom, who could not take the trouble to remember that three lumps was what Mr Lake liked
enrichment.summary: Lucilla is nearly overwhelmed with indignation at Barbara's failure to remember her father takes three lumps of sugar in his tea.

text:
Miss Marjoribanks had never taken tea with him before; but his second
cup, had she dispensed it, would have been exactly to his taste—which
was a thing Barbara had not learned to make it in all these years. No
wonder that a certain sense of contemptuous indignation arose for one
moment, even in the calm and impartial bosom of genius.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's detailed knowledge of Mr Lake's preferences, combined with her contempt for Barbara's ignorance, emphasizes her superior management and social awareness.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla knows Mr Lake's tea preferences despite having never taken tea with him, whereas Barbara has not learned them in years.

text:
Perhaps Rose
would not have done much better; but then Rose was good for something
else, which was always a set-off on the other side.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief comparative observation that Rose might be equally bad at tea service, but serves a larger point about her usefulness.
enrichment.summary: Rose might not be better at serving tea, but she is useful for other things.

text:
Thus it will be seen
that Lucilla had a respect for use, even of a kind which in her own
person she did not much appreciate, as became a person of a truly
enlightened mind; but a creature who was of no earthly good irritated
her well-regulated spirit; for, to be sure, the possession of a fine
contralto (which is, at the same time, not fine enough to be made use of
professionally) is not a matter of sufficient moment in this world to
excuse a young woman for not knowing how to give her father a
comfortable cup of tea.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brilliant satirical paragraph that critiques Barbara's usefulness, emphasizing the novel's concern with practical value and social utility.
enrichment.best_quote: the possession of a fine contralto (which is, at the same time, not fine enough to be made use of professionally) is not a matter of sufficient moment in this world to excuse a young woman for not knowing how to give her father a comfortable cup of tea
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's irritation peaks as she reflects that Barbara's contralto voice does not excuse her incompetence in the practical duty of serving tea.

text:
It was nearly nine o'clock before Mr Lake went out for his walk, and by
that time it was almost dark, and the lamp outside was lighted, which
was not far from the door. Lucilla had taken a seat near the window,
with the view of witnessing everything; and it cannot be denied that she
felt a little excited when Barbara went out of the room after her
father, leaving Rose alone with her guest.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shifts the narrative toward the climax: Mr Lake's departure creates the opportunity for the evening's main action, and Lucilla strategically positions herself to observe.
enrichment.summary: As evening falls, Mr Lake departs for his walk and Barbara leaves the room, leaving Lucilla alone with Rose and positioned to observe Grove Street through the window.

text:
Miss Marjoribanks's heart
gave a beat or two the more in the first minute, though before the next
had passed it had fallen into its usual measure.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief moment of excitement quickly suppressed, showing Lucilla's emotional discipline.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's heart quickens momentarily before returning to its usual measure.

text:
There were no candles
as yet in the parlour, and Grove Street—or at least the bit of it
which lay before the window, lighted by the lamp outside, and relieved
against a little square of bluish-green sky which intervened between
Miss Hemmings's house and that of old Mr Wrangle on the opposite
side—was very clear to the interested spectator.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid atmospheric description of Grove Street at twilight, establishing the visual stage for the clandestine encounter.
enrichment.best_quote: Grove Street—or at least the bit of it which lay before the window, lighted by the lamp outside, and relieved against a little square of bluish-green sky which intervened between Miss Hemmings's house and that of old Mr Wrangle on the opposite side—was very clear to the interested spectator
enrichment.summary: The street scene is clearly visible in the lamplight against a bluish-green twilight sky between the two opposing houses.

text:
There was nobody
visible but an organ-man, who was grinding a popular melody very
dolorously out of his box, in what Rose would have called the middle
distance; and beyond, Miss Jane Hemmings looking out of the long
staircase window, and three little boys in different attitudes
below,—that is, if one did not count a tall figure which, perhaps with
the view of listening to the music of the organ, was coming and going in
a limited circuit round the light of the lamp.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Detailed street observation that establishes the witnesses to the evening's action, creating dramatic irony about public observation and reputation.
enrichment.summary: The street shows Miss Hemmings at her staircase window, three boys below, an organ-man, and a tall figure circling the lamp, all potential observers.

text:
"How convenient it is to have the lamp so near," said Lucilla. "Oh,
don't light any candles, please; it is so nice to sit in the dark. Where
is Barbara, I wonder? Let us have some music, and put down that dreadful
organ. I hope she has not gone out. And where are you, you sulky little
Rose?"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla manipulates the scene by insisting on darkness and refusing candles, revealing her strategic control and desire to observe without being fully observed.
enrichment.best_quote: How convenient it is to have the lamp so near. Oh, don't light any candles, please; it is so nice to sit in the dark
enrichment.summary: Lucilla requests darkness and insists on using the street lamp as light, while questioning Barbara's whereabouts and asking for music.

text:
"She has gone upstairs," said Rose, who began to feel all the enormity
of her conduct in thus betraying her sister. "I hate sitting in the
dark. I hate being a spy; come in from the window, Lucilla, now you are
here——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rose's emotional distress and moral conflict are powerfully expressed as she recognizes the conspiratorial nature of the situation and her complicity.
enrichment.best_quote: She has gone upstairs. I hate sitting in the dark. I hate being a spy; come in from the window, Lucilla, now you are here——
enrichment.summary: Rose reveals Barbara's absence upstairs and expresses her hatred of her role as a spy and the darkness of her actions.

text:
"My dear Rose," said Miss Marjoribanks, "I think you forget a little. For my part I do not understand what being a spy means. Barbara knows
very well I am here. I should scorn to take an advantage of anybody, for
my part. If she does not bring him past the very window, and under my
eyes—Ah, yes, that is just what I thought," said Lucilla, with gentle
satisfaction.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's dismissal of Rose's moral concerns reveals her rationalization of surveillance and her confidence in Barbara's knowledge, demonstrating her power and conviction.
enrichment.best_quote: My dear Rose, I think you forget a little. For my part I do not understand what being a spy means. Barbara knows very well I am here. I should scorn to take an advantage of anybody, for my part.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla defends herself by claiming she scorn surveillance and that Barbara is aware of her presence, then watches expectantly.

text:
But by this time poor little Rose had roused herself into
an innocent fury.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief transition noting Rose's emotional response without significant new information.
enrichment.summary: Rose becomes angry in response to Lucilla's dismissal of her concerns.

text:
"What is just as you thought?" said Rose, laying an impatient grasp on
Miss Marjoribanks's arm. "Come in from the window, Lucilla, this
moment—this moment! Oh, me, to think it should be my doing! Oh,
Lucilla, don't be so mean and shabby and wretched. I tell you to come
in—come in directly! If you do not shut the window, and come and sit
here in the corner, I will never, never speak to you again!"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rose's passionate outburst reveals her genuine moral distress and desperate attempts to stop Lucilla, showing the psychological toll of the conspiracy.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh, Lucilla, don't be so mean and shabby and wretched. I tell you to come in—come in directly! If you do not shut the window, and come and sit here in the corner, I will never, never speak to you again!
enrichment.summary: Rose desperately pleads with Lucilla to leave the window and threatens never to speak to her again if she refuses.

text:
Miss Marjoribanks, as was natural, took no notice of this childish fury. She was sitting just where she had been sitting all the evening, within
sight of the street lamp and the organ-grinder, and Miss Jane Hemmings
at the staircase window;—just where Barbara had placed her, and where
that young woman calculated on finding her, when she made a promenade of
triumph up the partially lighted street by the side of her clandestine
suitor.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's unmoved composure and strategic positioning reveal her complete command of the situation, showing her as a manipulative orchestrator of events.
enrichment.best_quote: She was sitting just where she had been sitting all the evening, within sight of the street lamp and the organ-grinder, and Miss Jane Hemmings at the staircase window;—just where Barbara had placed her, and where that young woman calculated on finding her
enrichment.summary: Lucilla ignores Rose's pleas and remains positioned at the window to observe the street, as if Barbara had placed her there intentionally.

text:
Perhaps Barbara had seen Miss Jane as well, and knew that public
opinion was thus watching over her; but at all events she was not at all
ashamed of herself, or indignant at being spied upon. On the contrary,
it was a kind of apotheosis for Barbara, only second to the grand and
crowning triumph which would be accomplished in Carlingford Church under
the shadow of that veil of real Brussels, which grew more and more real
every day.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Barbara's shamelessness and her anticipation of her public 'triumph', showing the distinction between her values and those of respectable society.
enrichment.best_quote: it was a kind of apotheosis for Barbara, only second to the grand and crowning triumph which would be accomplished in Carlingford Church under the shadow of that veil of real Brussels, which grew more and more real every day
enrichment.summary: Barbara is unashamed of being spied upon; the public promenade with her lover is an apotheosis second only to her anticipated marriage.

text:
Thus neither the actors in the drama, nor the principal
spectator, were in the smallest degree disturbed by horror or shame or
sense of guilt, excepting always the fanciful little Rose, who suffered
for everybody; who could have wished that the earth would open and
swallow up Barbara and her lover; who could have slaughtered Lucilla on
the spot, and given herself over to any kind of torture for her
treachery. Naturally nobody paid any sort of attention to Rose.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A remarkable paragraph that crystallizes the psychological positions of all characters: Barbara and Lucilla unashamed, Cavendish weakly complicit, and Rose alone suffering from genuine moral shame.
enrichment.best_quote: Thus neither the actors in the drama, nor the principal spectator, were in the smallest degree disturbed by horror or shame or sense of guilt, excepting always the fanciful little Rose, who suffered for everybody; who could have wished that the earth would open and swallow up Barbara and her lover; who could have slaughtered Lucilla on the spot, and given herself over to any kind of torture for her treachery. Naturally nobody paid any sort of attention to Rose.
enrichment.summary: All characters lack shame except Rose, who agonizes over her complicity in the conspiracy while everyone ignores her moral distress.

text:
Barbara,
for her part, took her admirer's arm in the twilight with a swelling of
exultation, which the gaining of the very highest prize in the
department of ornamental art could scarcely have conveyed to the bosom
of the little artist; and Lucilla put back her small assailant softly
with her hand, and smoothed down her ruffled plumes.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Describes Barbara's exultation and Lucilla's dismissal of Rose's protest, emphasizing their contrasting emotional states and Lucilla's control.
enrichment.summary: Barbara takes her lover's arm with exultation while Lucilla gently restrains Rose with her hand and smooths her ruffled emotions.

text:
"My dear, it is Miss Hemmings that is spying," said Lucilla; "and poor
Barbara would be so disappointed if I were to go away from the window.
Have patience just a little longer—there's a dear. It is all exactly as
I thought."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla reassures Rose that it is Miss Hemmings who spies and asks for patience, continuing her manipulation while maintaining control.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reassures Rose that Miss Hemmings is the spy and asks Rose to be patient, assuring her that all is going according to plan.

text: And then there followed a pause, which was a terrible pause for Rose.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief transition indicating the psychological impact on Rose without new information.
enrichment.summary: A terrible silence follows as Rose waits in anguish.

text:
The organ-grinder stopped his doleful ditty, and there was scarcely any
sound to be heard in the street except the footsteps approaching and
retiring, the measured tread of two people occupied with each other,
going now more slowly, now more quickly, as the humour seized them, or
as their conversation grew in interest; even the sound of their voices
came by times to the auditors—Barbara's with an occasional laugh or
tone of triumph, and the other deeper, with which Rose had but little
acquaintance, but which was perfectly known to Lucilla.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid sensory description of the lovers' promenade, blending atmosphere with psychological insight into Lucilla's complete knowledge of Cavendish.
enrichment.best_quote: The organ-grinder stopped his doleful ditty, and there was scarcely any sound to be heard in the street except the footsteps approaching and retiring, the measured tread of two people occupied with each other, going now more slowly, now more quickly, as the humour seized them, or as their conversation grew in interest; even the sound of their voices came by times to the auditors—Barbara's with an occasional laugh or tone of triumph, and the other deeper, with which Rose had but little acquaintance, but which was perfectly known to Lucilla
enrichment.summary: The organ stops and the lovers' footsteps and voices are heard, Barbara laughing triumphantly while Cavendish's deeper voice is well-known to Lucilla.

text:
All this time,
while her companion sat panting in the dark corner, Miss Marjoribanks
was looking to the joints of her harness, and feeling the edge of her
weapons. For, after all, it was no small enterprise upon which she was
going forth.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brilliantly figurative passage that transforms Lucilla into a knight-errant preparing for battle, revealing her dramatization of her mission and absolute conviction in her righteousness.
enrichment.best_quote: All this time, while her companion sat panting in the dark corner, Miss Marjoribanks was looking to the joints of her harness, and feeling the edge of her weapons
enrichment.summary: As Rose pants in distress, Lucilla mentally prepares herself for the confrontation like a knight checking her armor and weapons.

text:
She was going to denounce the faithless knight to his face,
and take him out of the hands of the enchantress; but then she herself
meant to take him in hand, and show him his true dangers, and vindicate
his honour. A more disinterested enterprise was never undertaken by any
knight-errant.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's mission is explicitly stated in epic language that mocks her pretensions to disinterestedness while revealing her true motives of control and vindication.
enrichment.best_quote: She was going to denounce the faithless knight to his face, and take him out of the hands of the enchantress; but then she herself meant to take him in hand, and show him his true dangers, and vindicate his honour. A more disinterested enterprise was never undertaken by any knight-errant.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla plans to confront Cavendish and remove him from Barbara's influence, presenting this in deliberately grand and ironic language.

text:
Yet, at the same time, Lucilla could not help
entertaining a certain involuntary contempt for the man who had deserted
her own standard to put himself under that of Barbara Lake, and who was
being paraded up and down here without knowing it, to gratify the vanity
of his new sovereign, and make an exhibition of his weakness.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Lucilla's contempt for Cavendish beneath her ostensible magnanimity, showing her true motivations are mixed with disdain for his weakness.
enrichment.best_quote: Yet, at the same time, Lucilla could not help entertaining a certain involuntary contempt for the man who had deserted her own standard to put himself under that of Barbara Lake, and who was being paraded up and down here without knowing it, to gratify the vanity of his new sovereign
enrichment.summary: Lucilla secretly despises Cavendish for abandoning her influence for Barbara's and for allowing himself to be displayed as a trophy.

text:
Lucilla
would have been more than mortal if she had not felt the difference
between her own rule, which would have been all to his good, and the
purely egotistical sway of Barbara; and even in her magnanimous mind, it
was impossible that pity itself should not be mingled with a certain
disdain.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's self-awareness about the mixture of pity and disdain reveals the complexity of her motivations and the limits of her magnanimity.
enrichment.best_quote: Lucilla would have been more than mortal if she had not felt the difference between her own rule, which would have been all to his good, and the purely egotistical sway of Barbara; and even in her magnanimous mind, it was impossible that pity itself should not be mingled with a certain disdain
enrichment.summary: Lucilla is aware that her pity for Cavendish is mingled with disdain, as she contrasts her own rule with Barbara's selfish influence.

text:
She sat quite still for so long that Barbara grew intoxicated with her
triumph. "It is perhaps the last time," Lucilla said to herself, with a
movement of compassion; and the breadth of her human sympathy was such
that she waited till the very latest moment, and let the deluded young
woman have the full enjoyment of her imaginary victory.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's strategic patience and her apparent compassion are revealed as calculated moves, showing her complete control and her willingness to prolong Barbara's happiness.
enrichment.best_quote: She sat quite still for so long that Barbara grew intoxicated with her triumph. "It is perhaps the last time," Lucilla said to herself, with a movement of compassion; and the breadth of her human sympathy was such that she waited till the very latest moment, and let the deluded young woman have the full enjoyment of her imaginary victory.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla waits deliberately to let Barbara enjoy her false triumph to the last moment before acting, demonstrating calculated compassion and control.

text:
Then Miss
Marjoribanks rose with a certain solemnity, and put on her hat, and gave
an unappreciated kiss to Rose, who kept in her corner. "Good-night; I am
going," said Lucilla. The words were simple enough, but yet they rang in
Rose's ears like the signal of a conspiracy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's dramatic exit and her kiss to unappreciated Rose signal the conspiracy's culmination, with the simple words carrying enormous weight and ironic significance.
enrichment.best_quote: "Good-night; I am going," said Lucilla. The words were simple enough, but yet they rang in Rose's ears like the signal of a conspiracy.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla kisses the still-distressed Rose and announces her departure in simple words that signal the beginning of her intervention.

text:
When the calm leader of the
expedition went forth, sensible of the importance of her mission, but
tranquil as great minds always are in a moment of danger, Rose got up
too and followed, trembling in every limb. She was capable of having
thrown herself upon the spears in her own person in a sudden  élan  of
indignation and passion; but she was not capable of waiting till the
right moment, and meeting her antagonists in reasonable combat.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Contrasts Lucilla's calm composure with Rose's trembling anxiety, revealing the emotional disparity between the calculating leader and the morally sensitive follower.
enrichment.best_quote: When the calm leader of the expedition went forth, sensible of the importance of her mission, but tranquil as great minds always are in a moment of danger, Rose got up too and followed, trembling in every limb. She was capable of having thrown herself upon the spears in her own person in a sudden élan of indignation and passion; but she was not capable of waiting till the right moment, and meeting her antagonists in reasonable combat.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla leaves with calm composure while Rose follows trembling, able to act passionately but not strategically.

text:
Miss
Marjoribanks went out deliberately, without any unnecessary haste,
sweeping into the dusky twilight with her virginal white draperies. It
was a very ordinary scene, and yet, even in the midst of her excitement,
Rose could not help observing involuntarily its pictorial qualities—if
only any painter could have transferred to his canvas the subdued
musical hum of surrounding life, the fragrance of the mignonette, and
the peaceful stillness of the summer night.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A masterfully evocative passage that captures the moment's pictorial beauty through Rose's perception, blending sensory details with romantic imagery despite the moral sordidness of the situation.
enrichment.best_quote: It was a very ordinary scene, and yet, even in the midst of her excitement, Rose could not help observing involuntarily its pictorial qualities—if only any painter could have transferred to his canvas the subdued musical hum of surrounding life, the fragrance of the mignonette, and the peaceful stillness of the summer night.
enrichment.summary: Rose observes the beauty of the twilight scene despite her emotional turmoil, noting the fragrance of mignonette and peaceful summer air.

text:
The sky shone out
green-blue, lambent and wistful, from the vacant space between Miss
Hemmings's and Mr Wrangle's, and there were the dusky twilight shadows
below, and the yellow gleam of the lamp, and Barbara's exulting,
triumphant figure, and the white robes of the avenging angel.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Deeply literary and atmospheric, describing the scene as if composed by a painter, with symbolic colors and images that elevate the moment to mythic proportions.
enrichment.best_quote: The sky shone out green-blue, lambent and wistful, from the vacant space between Miss Hemmings's and Mr Wrangle's, and there were the dusky twilight shadows below, and the yellow gleam of the lamp, and Barbara's exulting, triumphant figure, and the white robes of the avenging angel.
enrichment.summary: The scene is painted in vivid colors: green-blue sky, shadows, yellow lamplight, Barbara's triumph, and Lucilla's white dress like an avenging angel.

text:
Rose could
not have observed all this if she had not been stilled into a kind of
breathless awe by the solemn character of the situation, which struck
her as being somehow like one of Millais's pictures. As for the lovers,
they had just turned at the moment that Miss Marjoribanks came out, and
consequently met her straight in the face, as she stood suave and
smiling at the little garden door.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The climactic moment where Lucilla and the lovers meet; the comparison to Millais's paintings elevates the scene to high art, emphasizing the theatrical and pictorial nature of the moment.
enrichment.best_quote: Rose could not have observed all this if she had not been stilled into a kind of breathless awe by the solemn character of the situation, which struck her as being somehow like one of Millais's pictures. As for the lovers, they had just turned at the moment that Miss Marjoribanks came out, and consequently met her straight in the face, as she stood suave and smiling at the little garden door.
enrichment.summary: Rose perceives the scene as if painted by Millais just as the lovers turn to face Lucilla emerging from the garden door.

text:
"It  is  Mr Cavendish," said Lucilla; "I am so glad; I have been hoping
and trying to see you for ever so long; and as soon as ever I heard you
talking I felt sure it was your voice."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's opening gambit is masterful: she greets Cavendish as if surprised, claiming she had been hoping to see him, immediately seizing the initiative and establishing her narrative.
enrichment.best_quote: "It is Mr Cavendish," said Lucilla; "I am so glad; I have been hoping and trying to see you for ever so long; and as soon as ever I heard you talking I felt sure it was your voice."
enrichment.summary: Lucilla greets Cavendish with apparent surprise and delight, claiming she had been trying to see him and recognized his voice.

text:
This was the greeting she addressed to Barbara Lake's lover. For his
part he stood before her, growing red and growing pale, struck dumb by
the unlooked-for meeting, and with such a sense of being ashamed of
himself as never before had entered his mind, though, no doubt, he had
done worse actions in his day.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's shocked reaction is graphically rendered, showing how Lucilla's sudden appearance has unmanned him and filled him with shame.
enrichment.best_quote: For his part he stood before her, growing red and growing pale, struck dumb by the unlooked-for meeting, and with such a sense of being ashamed of himself as never before had entered his mind, though, no doubt, he had done worse actions in his day.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish is struck dumb, blushing and paling with shame at being caught in the compromising position.

text:
Even Barbara had not calculated upon this
open encounter; and instead of giving him any assistance, as was a
woman's duty in such a case, she only tossed her head, and giggled with
an embarrassment which was more pride than shame. As for Mr Cavendish,
he would have liked to disappear under the pavement, if it had been
possible. For once he and Rose were agreed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barbara's shameless reaction and Cavendish's desire to disappear reveal the contrasting character values and Cavendish's moral weakness.
enrichment.best_quote: Even Barbara had not calculated upon this open encounter; and instead of giving him any assistance, as was a woman's duty in such a case, she only tossed her head, and giggled with an embarrassment which was more pride than shame. As for Mr Cavendish, he would have liked to disappear under the pavement, if it had been possible. For once he and Rose were agreed.

Mrs Centum who were coming down behind him—she with a light shawl
thrown over her head, tempted out by the beauty of the evening; and
Lucilla saw in a moment the consequences of this encounter, and how it
would be over all Carlingford before to-morrow morning that she and Mr
Cavendish were betrothed at the very least. Miss Marjoribanks had all
her wits about her, as ever, fortunately for both.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla immediately perceives the social consequences of the encounter and the gossip it will generate; she will spin a story to redirect Carlingford's interpretation.

Miss Marjoribanks had all her wits about her, as ever, fortunately for both.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla instantly recognizes the gossip this encounter will generate and that Carlingford will assume she and Cavendish are betrothed.

"Yes, it is me," she said calmly; "I have been taking tea with the
Lakes, and I made Mr Cavendish give me his arm home. He did not like
being found out, to be sure, but he could not help himself; and we all
know about that," Lucilla added, with a smile, taking once more the
unfortunate man's arm.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's quick narrative reframes the situation, claiming Cavendish walked her home from tea, reversing what actually happened and establishing her as the active subject.

text:
"Oh, yes, we all know," said Mrs Centum, with a
laugh; but yet, notwithstanding, everybody felt sure that it was all
Lucilla's cleverness, and that Barbara Lake was a myth and fiction.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs Centum's laugh and implicit disbelief suggest that Carlingford will credit Lucilla's narrative while dismissing Barbara as a myth.
enrichment.summary: Mrs Centum's reaction implies she disbelieves Lucilla's account but will spread it, rendering Barbara's attachment as fictional.

text:
And
it was thus, with Miss Marjoribanks leaning on his arm, and General
Travers, in all the warmth of renewed friendship, guarding him on the
other side, that Mr Cavendish, whose head was in a whirl of excitement,
and who did not know what he was doing, was led back in triumph past
Colonel Chiley's very door, where the Archdeacon was lying in wait to
crunch his bones, back from all his aberrations into the very heart of
Grange Lane.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The final triumphant paragraph synthesizes the chapter's arc: Cavendish is led in triumph past the Archdeacon's house, back to Grange Lane, fully under Lucilla's control and restored to his proper sphere.
enrichment.best_quote: And it was thus, with Miss Marjoribanks leaning on his arm, and General Travers, in all the warmth of renewed friendship, guarding him on the other side, that Mr Cavendish, whose head was in a whirl of excitement, and who did not know what he was doing, was led back in triumph past Colonel Chiley's very door, where the Archdeacon was lying in wait to crunch his bones, back from all his aberrations into the very heart of Grange Lane.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish is led in triumph by Lucilla and General Travers past the Archdeacon's position and back to Grange Lane, fully restored under Lucilla's influence.

text:
Mr Cavendish was led back to his own house that evening by General
Travers, whose claim of acquaintance was too decided to be rejected. He
never knew very well what passed between the moment when Miss
Marjoribanks began to expound to him the urgent necessity that he should
confide in her, and the moment in which he found himself in his own
house, admitted eagerly by the surprised and anxious servants, and
conducted by the energetic soldier.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes setting and characters but primarily expository connective prose moving Cavendish from Lucilla's house to his own.
enrichment.summary: General Travers accompanies Cavendish home after an evening at the Marjoribanks residence, with Cavendish remaining dazed about the events that transpired.

text:
That he had taken leave of Lucilla
at her own door, that he had watched her white dress sweep away into the
dark garden with a faint sense that it was his only remaining protector
who thus left him, and that after that he had smoked a horrible cigar
with Mr Centum, and been accompanied home by the old acquaintance, who
had turned up at so unlucky a moment,—was all that the poor man was
aware of.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Cavendish's emotional state and his perception of Lucilla as a protective figure, hinting at underlying anxiety.
enrichment.best_quote: his only remaining protector

text:
And yet it is to be supposed that on the whole he behaved
himself very much like other people, since General Travers had no

recognition was anything but welcome. The General, indeed, took it as
quite natural, under the circumstances, that Cavendish should be a
little confused.

A man who is no longer a very young man, and has a
character to support, does not care to be found mooning with the object

It

It's immense luck to find you here, Cavendish," General Travers
added, with flattering cordiality; and if poor Mr Cavendish was not
grateful, it certainly was not his friend's fault. He led the way into
his house with a glum countenance and a sinking heart, though

He had some nice pictures and a good library, though he was not
particularly given to the arts; and he had an admirable cellar, as all
the gentlemen owned in Carlingford, though, for his own part, he was
very moderate in that point, and did not give himself any airs on the

And General
Travers could not but feel the force of the contrast as he sat deep into
the night, and "talked over everything," with the man who by that time
he felt convinced was one of his best friends.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Concluding observation about General Travers's feeling of friendship, mere connective prose with no significant information.

As for Mr Cavendish, it would be very difficult to describe his

text:
He was
preoccupied to the last degree, wondering what Miss Marjoribanks really
knew, and how far he had betrayed himself, and to what extent it would
be safe, as she herself said, to confide in Lucilla; and at the same
time he was obliged to listen to and show a certain interest in the

text:

"To be candid, I don't
call her strictly handsome, you know; she's too big for that—and I
don't suppose she's of any family to speak of; though perhaps you don't
mind that trifling circumstance; but a woman that will dress well and

"I am sure I am much obliged to you," said Mr Cavendish, "though,
unfortunately, I don't merit your approbation. Miss Marjoribanks is a
great friend of mine, but she wouldn't have me, and I don't mean to ask
her. At the same time, she has very good connections; and that is not
the way to talk of a girl of twenty. She is worth a dozen of your fast
young ladies," said the sufferer, with some heat.

He was not in the

this present moment; but he could not forget that she had once stood by
him in his need—and, besides, he was glad of any subject on which he
could contradict his visitor. "I dare say her family is better than
either yours or mine. Scotch, you know," said Mr Cavendish, trying to
laugh.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Clarifies Cavendish's relationship with Lucilla and his lingering gratitude, while explaining his relief in finding an outlet for contradiction.
enrichment.best_quote: she had once stood by him in his need

at liberty to forget a woman when other matters of more immediate
interest are absorbing his attention, and yet be driven furious by the
idea suddenly presented to him that somebody else, who has nothing
earthly to do with it, is about to interfere. Mr Cavendish, however,

representing a town without saying a single word about his principles.

not to leave you  that  all to yourselves, I don't know what you could

Mr Cavendish, that he could not believe in her desertion in his heart.

 had  gone off, whatever she herself might have done.
