When they had done, he got down off his seat and took his
right hand out of his pocket and offered it to Miss Brown, who, putting
her own into it, poor soul! with the remembrance of her ancient
allegiance, was like to cry.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's gracious departure gesture to Maria and her emotional response hint at the pathos beneath the comedy.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish extends his hand to Maria, who takes it with remembered affection and near-tears.

text:
"Well," he said, "if that is the case, I suppose I need not bother you
any longer. You'll give me your good wishes all the same. I used to hear
of Ashburton sometimes, but I never had the least idea he was so
popular. And to tell the truth, I don't think he's any great things to
brag of—though I suppose it's not to be expected  I  should appreciate
his qualities," Mr Cavendish added, with a laugh.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish exits with forced wit about Ashburton, maintaining pride while revealing his wounded feeling and dismissive competitiveness.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish offers graceful thanks and dismisses Ashburton as unimpressive, concealing his disappointment.

text:
As for Miss Brown, it
was all she could do to keep from crying as he went away. She said she
could see, by the way he left the drawing-room, that he was a stricken
deer; and yet, notwithstanding this sympathetic feeling, she could not
but acknowledge, when Miss Marjoribanks mentioned it, that, to have been
such a handsome man, he was inconceivably gone off.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Maria's emotional response and later observation to Lucilla about Cavendish's decline deliver sharp social irony—she pities him but judges him harshly.
enrichment.best_quote: She said she could see, by the way he left the drawing-room, that he was a stricken deer
enrichment.summary: Maria nearly cries as Cavendish leaves, but later remarks to Lucilla that despite having been handsome, he has inconceivably aged.

text:
Mr Cavendish went up Grange Lane with his hands in his pockets, and
tried to think that he did not care; but he did care all the same, and
was very bitter in his mind over the failure of friends and the vanity
of expectations. The last time he had walked past those garden walls he
had thought himself sure of the support of Carlingford, and the
personal esteem of all the people in all the houses he was passing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's solitary reflection on betrayal and lost expectations introduces a melancholic turn; the contrast with his confident past heightens the tragedy.
enrichment.best_quote: he did care all the same, and was very bitter in his mind over the failure of friends and the vanity of expectations
enrichment.summary: Cavendish walks through Carlingford pretending indifference but bitterly reflecting on the failure of his former friends and his own expectations.

text:
It
was after the Archdeacon had broken down in his case against the man
whom he called an adventurer, and when Mr Cavendish felt all the
sweetness of being a member of an oligarchy, and entitled to the
sympathy and support of his order. Now he went along the same path with
his hat over his ears and his hands in his pockets, and rage and pain in
his heart.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator contrasts Cavendish's past confident belonging as member of an oligarchy with his present isolated despair, exposing social hierarchy's cruelty.
enrichment.best_quote: when Mr Cavendish felt all the sweetness of being a member of an oligarchy, and entitled to the sympathy and support of his order
enrichment.summary: The narrator recalls how Cavendish previously basked in oligarchic privilege after the Archdeacon's courtroom defeat, contrasting with his current isolation.

text:
Whose fault was it that his friends had deserted him and
Carlingford knew him no more? He might as well have asked whose fault it
was that he was getting stout and red in the face, and had not the same
grace of figure nor ease of mind as he used to have?

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator delivers a penetrating rhetorical question linking Cavendish's social failure to his physical decline—a masterful summation of his ruined life.
enrichment.best_quote: Whose fault was it that his friends had deserted him and Carlingford knew him no more? He might as well have asked whose fault it was that he was getting stout and red in the face, and had not the same grace of figure nor ease of mind as he used to have?
enrichment.summary: The narrator connects Cavendish's loss of social standing to his physical deterioration, implying both are consequences of his own choices.

text:
He had come very
near to settling down and becoming a man of domestic respectability in
this quiet place, and he had just escaped in time, and had laughed over
it since, and imagined himself, with much glee, an old fogy looking
after a lot of children.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish reflects on escaping domestic respectability in Carlingford, revealing how he deluded himself about his life choices and trajectory.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish recalls that he nearly settled into domestic life in Carlingford but escaped and considered himself fortunate.

text:
But the fact is that men do become old fogies
even when they have no children to look after, and lose their figure and
their elasticity just as soon and perhaps a little sooner in the midst
of what is called life than in any milder scene of enjoyment. And it
would have been very handy just now to have been sure of his election
without paying much for it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator delivers a devastating commentary on male aging and decline, suggesting that dissipation ages men faster than domestic quiet—a profound moral indictment.
enrichment.best_quote: men do become old fogies even when they have no children to look after, and lose their figure and their elasticity just as soon and perhaps a little sooner in the midst of what is called life than in any milder scene of enjoyment
enrichment.summary: The narrator comments that men age and decline from a life of excess just as readily as from domestic routines.

text:
He had been living fast, and spending a
great deal of money, and this, after all, was the only real ambition he
had ever had; and he had thought within himself that if he won he would
change his mode of life, and turn over a new leaf, and become all at
once a different man.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's reflection reveals his financial desperation and moral delusion—election victory is merely cover for a life of excess spent at ruinous pace.
enrichment.best_quote: He had been living fast, and spending a great deal of money, and this, after all, was the only real ambition he had ever had
enrichment.summary: The narrator reveals that Cavendish's reckless living and spending have driven his desperate ambition for election.

text:
When a man has made such a resolution, and feels
not only that a mere success but a moral reformation depends upon his
victory, he may be permitted to consider that he has a right to win; and
it may be divined what his state of mind was when he had made the
discovery that even his old friends did not see his election to be of
any such importance as he did, and could think of a miserable little bit
of self-importance or gratified vanity more than of his interests—even
the women who had once been so kind to him!

enrichment.interest_rationale: A profound indictment of Cavendish's self-justified hypocrisy—he demands victory as moral reward while his friends see his vanity, not virtue.
enrichment.best_quote: When a man has made such a resolution, and feels not only that a mere success but a moral reformation depends upon his victory, he may be permitted to consider that he has a right to win
enrichment.summary: The narrator exposes how Cavendish justifies his electoral claim as moral necessity while his friends merely see his selfish vanity.

text:
He had just got so far in
his thoughts when he met Mr Centum, who stared for a moment, and then
burst into one of his great laughs as he greeted him. "Good Lord! Cavendish, is this you? I never expected to see you like that!" the
banker said, in his coarse way.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Centum's arrival and crude greeting about Cavendish's weight introduces another humiliation, maintaining comic tone but deepening pathos.
enrichment.summary: Mr Centum encounters Cavendish and bluntly comments on how much he has changed, calling him stouter than before.

text:
"You're stouter than I am, old fellow;
and such an Adonis as you used to be!" Mr Cavendish had to bear all this
without giving way to his feelings, or even showing them any more than
he could help it. Nobody would spare him that imbecile suggestion as to
how things used to be.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Centum's continuing tactless remarks about Cavendish's lost attractiveness deliver repeated blows, though Cavendish endures silently for political necessity.
enrichment.summary: Centum comments crudely on how much more stout and less handsome Cavendish has become.

text:
To be growing stouter than Centum without
Centum's excuse of being a well-to-do householder and father of a
family, and respectable man from whom stoutness was expected, was very
bitter to him: but he had to gulp it down, and recollect that Centum was
as yet the only influential supporter, except his brother-in-law, whom
he had in Carlingford.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's bitterness at being stouter than Centum while lacking his social excuse (wife, children, respectability) reveals class dynamics and his moral ruin.
enrichment.best_quote: To be growing stouter than Centum without Centum's excuse of being a well-to-do householder and father of a family, and respectable man from whom stoutness was expected, was very bitter to him
enrichment.summary: The narrator explains Cavendish's bitter humiliation: he is corpulent without the social legitimacy of respectability that would excuse it.

text:
"What have you been doing with yourself since you came that nobody has
seen you?" said Mr Centum. "If you are to do any good here, you know, we
shall have to look alive."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Centum asks practical electoral questions about Cavendish's activity, advancing campaign logistics without distinctive content.
enrichment.summary: Centum questions why Cavendish has not been visible and urges him to be more active in campaigning.

text:
"I have been ill," said the unfortunate candidate, with a little natural
loss of temper. "You would not have a man to trudge about at this time
of year in all weathers when he is ill."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's excuse of illness and mild irritation is routine; the narrator notes his loss of temper, revealing weakness.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish defensively claims he has been ill and unable to campaign actively.

text:
"I would not be ill again, if I were you, till it's all over," said Mr
Centum. "We shall have to fight every inch of our ground; and I tell you
that fellow Ashburton knows what he's about—he goes at everything in a
steady sort of way. He's not brilliant, you know, but he's sure——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Centum dismisses Cavendish's illness excuse and warns about Ashburton's formidable, systematic campaign approach—a realistic assessment of electoral competition.
enrichment.summary: Centum advises Cavendish not to be ill during the campaign and warns that Ashburton is a formidable opponent with steady method.

text:
"Brilliant!" said Mr Cavendish, "I should think not. It is Lucilla
Marjoribanks who is putting him up to it. You know she had an old grudge
at me."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish blames Lucilla Marjoribanks for Ashburton's candidacy, revealing his resentment of her influence and confirming her orchestration.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish claims Lucilla Marjoribanks is manipulating Ashburton against him out of old resentment.

text:
"Oh, nonsense about Lucilla," said Mr Centum. "I can tell you Ashburton
is not at all a contemptible adversary. He is going to work in the
cunningest way—not a woman's sort of thing, and he's not a ladies' man
like you," the banker added, with a laugh.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Centum dismisses Lucilla's role and praises Ashburton's systematic method, implicitly contrasting it with Cavendish's superficial 'ladies' man' approach.
enrichment.summary: Centum dismisses Lucilla's influence and credits Ashburton's steady, non-superficial campaign method.

text:
"But I am afraid you can't go in for that sort of thing as you used to
do, Cavendish. You should marry, and settle, and become a steady member
of society, now you've grown so stout." This was the kind of way in
which he was addressed even by his own supporter, who uttered another
great laugh as he went off upon his busy way.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Centum advises Cavendish to marry and settle, but his crude laughter undercuts any sincerity, exposing how even allies mock Cavendish's decline.
enrichment.best_quote: You should marry, and settle, and become a steady member of society, now you've grown so stout
enrichment.summary: Centum crudely suggests Cavendish marry and become respectable, laughing at his own suggestion.

text:
It was a sort of thing Mr
Cavendish was not used to, and he felt it accordingly. To be sure he
knew that he was ten years older, and that there were several things
which he could not do with the same facility as in his youth.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish acknowledges his aging but defensively rationalizes his decline, exposing his insecurity about physical change.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish concedes he has aged ten years and lost his youthful abilities, though he struggles with the reality.

text:
But he had
saved up Carlingford in his imagination as a spot in which he would
always be young, and where nobody should find out the difference; and
instead of that, it was precisely in Carlingford that he was fated to
hear how changed he was, with a frankness which only old friends would
have been justified in using. As for Lucilla Marjoribanks, she was
rather better looking than otherwise, and absolutely had not gone off.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish had imagined Carlingford as timeless sanctuary where youth persisted; instead it brutally exposes his decline, while Lucilla paradoxically thrives.
enrichment.best_quote: he had saved up Carlingford in his imagination as a spot in which he would always be young, and where nobody should find out the difference
enrichment.summary: Cavendish's illusion of Carlingford as a timeless refuge shattered; ironically, Lucilla remains beautiful while he has visibly declined.

text:
It did not occur to Mr Cavendish that this might be because Lucilla at
present was not still so old as he had been ten years ago, in the period
which he now considered his youth. He was rather disposed, on the
contrary, to take a moral view, and to consider that it was her feminine
incapacity for going too far, which had kept years and amusements from
having their due effect upon Miss Marjoribanks.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator uses Lucilla as foil to expose Cavendish's self-serving moral judgment—he attributes her beauty to virtue while blaming his own decline on excess.
enrichment.best_quote: he was rather disposed, on the contrary, to take a moral view, and to consider that it was her feminine incapacity for going too far, which had kept years and amusements from having their due effect upon Miss Marjoribanks
enrichment.summary: Cavendish moralizes that Lucilla's feminine virtue preserved her, while implicitly damning himself for masculine excess.

text:
And, poor fellow, he
 had  gone too far. He had not been as careful in his life as he might
have been had he stayed at Carlingford; and now he was paying the
penalty. Such was the edifying state of mind which he had come to when
he reached the top of Grove Street. And there a waft of soft
recollections came across his mind.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator summarizes Cavendish's self-aware moral reckoning—he recognizes he 'had gone too far'—before introducing the memory of Lucilla as potential refuge.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish reflects on his moral decline and how he is suffering the consequences of excess, then recalls memories of Lucilla.

text:
In the absence of all sympathy he
could not help turning back to the thought of the enchantress of old who
used to sing to him, and listen to him, and storm at him. Probably he
would have ended by strolling along the familiar street, and canvassing
for Mr Lake's vote, which would have done him no good in Carlingford,
but just then Dr Marjoribanks stopped in his brougham.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's nostalgia for Lucilla as 'enchantress' who sang, listened, and quarreled—the only source of sympathy in his isolation—evokes pathos and suggests lingering attachment.
enrichment.best_quote: the thought of the enchantress of old who used to sing to him, and listen to him, and storm at him
enrichment.summary: Isolated and without sympathy, Cavendish turns his thoughts to Lucilla Marjoribanks, remembering her as an enchantress before her father's carriage interrupts.

text:
The Doctor was
looking very strange that morning, though nobody had particularly
remarked it—perhaps because he smoothed his countenance when he was out
of the brougham, which was his refuge when he had anything to think
about. But he stopped suddenly to speak to Mr Cavendish, and perhaps he
had not time to perform that ceremony.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor appears unexpectedly troubled but attempting to conceal it; his stopping Cavendish suggests both sympathy and burden.
enrichment.summary: Dr Marjoribanks stops his carriage to speak with Cavendish, appearing troubled despite his efforts to conceal it.

text:
He looked dark and cloudy, and
constrained, and as if he forced himself to speak; which, to be sure,
under the circumstances, was not so very strange.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor's dark, cloudy appearance is described but without significant content—routine physical observation.
enrichment.summary: The narrator describes the Doctor's dark, constrained demeanor.

text:
"I am very glad to see you," the Doctor said, "though you were a day too
late, you know. Why didn't you give us warning before we all went and
committed ourselves? If we had known that you were coming——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor repeats the Major's excuse about Cavendish's late return and lack of warning, maintaining narrative consistency about Ashburton's unexpected candidacy.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor regrets that Cavendish arrived too late to prevent his friends from committing to Ashburton.

text:
"Ah, that's what old Brown said," said Mr Cavendish, with a slight shrug
of his shoulders; which was imprudent, for the Major was not so old as
the Doctor, and besides was a much less important man in Grange Lane.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish dismissively compares the Doctor to Major Brown, a minor social error that reveals his bitterness without significance.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish carelessly compares the Doctor to Major Brown, implying the Doctor's inferior importance.

text:
"So you have been to see old Brown," said Dr Marjoribanks, in his dry
way. "He always was a great admirer of yours. I can't wish you luck, you
know, for if you win we lose——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor dryly confirms he saw the Major and openly states his opposition: if Cavendish wins, he loses—a frank acknowledgment of electoral stakes.
enrichment.best_quote: I can't wish you luck, you know, for if you win we lose
enrichment.summary: The Doctor frankly tells Cavendish he cannot wish him luck because their electoral interests are opposed.

text:
"Oh, I don't want you to wish me luck. I don't suppose there can be much
comparison between my chance and that of a new man whom nobody ever
heard of in my time," said the candidate for Carlingford. "I thought you
Scotchmen, Doctor, always liked to be on the winning side."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish argues his superiority over Ashburton and makes a stereotype about Scots favoring winners, revealing his frustration and ethnic prejudice.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish dismisses Ashburton as unknown and accuses the Doctor of opportunistically backing winners.

text:
"We've a way of making our side the winning side," said Dr Marjoribanks
grimly, for he was touchy where his nationality was concerned. "Health
all right, I hope?" he added, looking at Mr Cavendish with that critical
medical glance which shows that a verbal response is quite unnecessary. This time there was in the look a certain insinuation of doubt on the
subject, which was not pleasant.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor's nationalist response and medical scrutiny of Cavendish's health deliver dual messages: defensiveness about Scotland and clinical concern about physical decline.
enrichment.best_quote: We've a way of making our side the winning side
enrichment.summary: The Doctor defends Scottish shrewdness and scrutinizes Cavendish's health with a medical gaze suggesting doubt.

text:
"You are getting stout, I see," Dr
Marjoribanks added—not laughing, but as if that too was poor Mr
Cavendish's fault.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor bluntly observes Cavendish's weight gain, delivering another public humiliation but delivered clinically and with implied blame.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor notes that Cavendish is stouter, not sympathetically but as if it is Cavendish's fault.

text:
"Yes, I'm very well," he answered curtly; but the truth was that he did
not feel sure that he was quite well after he had seen the critical look
in Dr Marjoribanks's eye.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish curtly affirms his health but internally doubts it after the Doctor's critical medical gaze—routine introspection without distinction.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish denies illness but becomes anxious after the Doctor's scrutiny.

text:
"You young men always go too fast," said the Doctor, with a strange
little smile; but the term at least was consolatory; and after that
Doctor Marjoribanks quite changed his tone. "Have you heard Woodburn
talking of that great crash in town?" he said—"that India house, you
know—I suppose it's quite true?"

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor pivots from health criticism to financial gossip about an India house crash, offering Cavendish the pleasure of sharing scandalous news.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor asks about a financial crash in town and mentions hearing Woodburn discuss it.

text:
"Quite true," said Mr Cavendish, promptly, and somehow he felt a
pleasure in saying it. "I got all the particulars to-day in one of my
letters—and lots of private people involved, which is always the way
with these old houses," he added, with a mixture of curiosity and
malice—"widows, and all sorts of superannuated folks."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish eagerly confirms the crash and maliciously identifies victims (widows, superannuated folks), revealing his capacity for schadenfreude and moral bankruptcy.
enrichment.best_quote: widows, and all sorts of superannuated folks
enrichment.summary: Cavendish eagerly shares details of the India house crash and its victims, mixing curiosity with malicious pleasure.

text:
"It's a great pity," said the Doctor: "I knew old Lichfield once, the
chief partner—I am very sorry to hear it's true;" and then the two
shook hands, and the brougham drove on. As for Mr Cavendish, he made up
his mind at once that the Doctor was involved, and was not sorry, and
felt that it was a sort of judicial recompense for his desertion of his
friends.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish infers the Doctor is personally involved in the crash and takes vengeful pleasure in his misfortune, seeing it as divine recompense for betrayal.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish deduces the Doctor is financially involved and takes malicious satisfaction in his suffering as just punishment.

text:
And he went home to tell his sister of it, who shared in his
sentiments. And then it was not worth while going out any more that
day—for the electioneering agent, who knew all about it, was not coming
till the last train. "I suppose I shall have to work when he is here,"
Mr Cavendish said. And in the meantime he threw himself into an easy
chair. Perhaps that was why he was getting so stout.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish goes home to share the scandal with his sister and then settles into leisure, the narrator noting this idleness may explain his weight gain.
enrichment.best_quote: Perhaps that was why he was getting so stout
enrichment.summary: Cavendish shares the financial scandal with his sister and settles into an easy chair, awaiting his agent.

text:
And in the meantime the Doctor went on visiting his patients. When he
came back to his brougham between his visits, and went bowling along in
that comfortable way, along the familiar roads, there was a certain
glumness upon his face.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shift to the Doctor's perspective: he continues visiting patients but shows glumness when alone, establishing that he carries a burden beyond his electoral opposition.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor visits his patients but displays glumness when alone in his carriage.

text:
He was not a demonstrative man, but when he was
alone you could tell by certain lines about the well-worn cordage of his
countenance whether all was right with the Doctor; and it was easy to
see just at this moment that all was not right with him. But he did not
say anything about it when he got home; on the contrary, he was just as
usual, and told his daughter all about his encounter with Mr Cavendish.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor conceals his troubles and reports his Cavendish encounter to Lucilla, maintaining his composed exterior despite internal strain.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor returns home and tells Lucilla about meeting Cavendish, showing no outward sign of his troubles.

text:
"A man at his time of life has no right to get fat—it's a sort of thing
I don't like to see. And he'll never be a ladies' man no more, Lucilla,"
said the Doctor, with a gleam of humour in his eye.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor comments to Lucilla that Cavendish's fatness is unseemly and destroys his ladies' man status, continuing the theme of decline but with humor.
enrichment.best_quote: A man at his time of life has no right to get fat—it's a sort of thing I don't like to see. And he'll never be a ladies' man no more, Lucilla
enrichment.summary: The Doctor remarks to Lucilla that Cavendish's fatness is improper and has ended his appeal to women.

text:
"He is exactly like George the Fourth, papa," said Miss Marjoribanks;
and the Doctor laughed as he sat down to dinner. If he had anything on
his mind he bore it like a hero, and gave no sign; but then, as Mrs John
very truly remarked, when a man does not disclose his annoyances they
always tell more upon him in the end.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's George IV comparison is witty; the Doctor laughs easily, yet the narrator notes he bears unspoken burdens silently—a poignant contrast.
enrichment.best_quote: He is exactly like George the Fourth, papa
enrichment.summary: Lucilla compares Cavendish to George IV; the Doctor laughs but the narrator notes he silently bears a burden that will ultimately harm him.

text:
There were a great many reasons why this should be a critical period in
Miss Marjoribanks's life. For one thing, it was the limit she had always
proposed to herself for her term of young-ladyhood; and naturally, as
she outgrew the age for them, she felt disposed to put away childish
things.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the chapter's central tension: Lucilla reaching her thirtieth year and the limit of her youthful role, prompting reflection on her future purpose.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla has reached the age she set as the limit for young-ladyhood and is beginning to outgrow childish pursuits.

text:
The talk of this evening might not have been considered of any
importance to speak of, but for the extraordinary and most unlooked-for
event which startled all Carlingford next morning. Nobody could believe
that it was true. Dr Marjoribanks's patients waited for him, and
declared to their nurses that it was all a made-up story, and that he
would come and prove that he was not dead. How could he be dead?

enrichment.interest_rationale: The unexpected death of Dr Marjoribanks is the central turning point of the novel, shocking Carlingford and upending Lucilla's position.
enrichment.summary: The news breaks that Dr Marjoribanks has died suddenly in the night, shocking all of Carlingford and casting doubt on the reality of the event.

text:
He had
been as well as he ever was that last evening. He had gone down Grange
Lane in the snow, to see the poor old lady who was now sobbing in her
bed, and saying it was all a mistake, and that it was she who ought to
have died. But all those protestations were of no avail against the cold
and stony fact which had frightened Thomas out of his senses, when he
went to call the Doctor.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Provides details of the Doctor's final evening and introduces the bereaved patient, Mrs Chiley, adding pathos to the revelation.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor had visited a poor elderly patient in the snow the previous evening and died that night, with the patient now blaming herself.

text:
He had died in the night without calling or
disturbing anybody. He must have felt faint, it seemed, for he had got
up and taken a little brandy, the remains of which still stood on the
table by his bedside; but that was all that anybody could tell about it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Details the Doctor's death, establishing it as sudden and peaceful, with minimal disturbance to the household.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor died quietly in bed, apparently taking brandy when he felt faint, disturbing no one in the household.

text:
They brought Dr Rider, of course; but all that he could do was to
examine the strong, still frame—old, and yet not old enough to be
weakly, or to explain such sudden extinction—which had ceased its human
functions. And then the news swept over Carlingford like a breath of
wind, though there was no wind even on that silent snowy day to carry
the matter. Dr Marjoribanks was dead.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dr Rider's examination and the rapid spread of news across Carlingford establish the community's shock and the finality of the event.
enrichment.summary: Dr Rider examines the body and confirms death; the news spreads throughout Carlingford on the silent snowy day.

text:
It put the election out of
people's heads, and even their own affairs for the time being; for had
he not known all about the greater part of them—seen them come into the
world and kept them in it—and put himself always in the breach when the
pale Death approached that way?

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the Doctor's crucial role in Carlingford's life and society, showing how his death disrupts even the election campaign.
enrichment.summary: The Doctor's death overshadows all other concerns including the election, as he was indispensable to Carlingford's life.

text:
He had never made very much boast of his
friendliness or been large in sympathetic expressions, but yet he had
never flinched at any time, or deserted his patients for any
consideration. Carlingford was sorry, profoundly sorry, with that true
sorrow which is not so much for the person mourned as for the mourner's
self, who feels a sense of something lost.

He was a man quite famous
for his extempore gifts, and who rather liked to preach about any very
recent public event, which it was evident to all his hearers could not
have found place in a "prepared" discourse; and his sermon that morning

text:
But it would be wrong to say that this was the general tone of public
opinion in Grove Street; most people, on the contrary, thought of Mr

text:
Such was the impression of a great many influential
persons who had been wavering hitherto, and inclining on the whole to Mr
Cavendish's liberal principles and supposed Low-Church views.

text:
A man
whose hand is red metaphorically with your sister's blood is no doubt a
highly objectionable personage; but it is doubtful whether, under the
circumstances, an enlightened constituency might not consider the man

enrichment.summary: Grange Lane's fury at Barbara's return is exceeded by George Street and Wharfside's scorn at the prospect of Cavendish marrying her, revealing class prejudice.

text:
Society had
nothing worse to say than to quote Mrs Chiley, and assert that "these
artist people were all adventurers"; and then Grange Lane in general
could not forget that it "had met" Barbara, nor dismiss from its
consideration her black eyes, her level brows, and her magnificent
contralto; whereas in the other region the idea of the Member for

delirium.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Character portrait of Barbara revealing working-class perception; details of her appearance and accomplishments that provoke snobbery.
enrichment.best_quote: these artist people were all adventurers

text:
It was a still more deadly offence to the small people than to
the great. And the exceptional standing which poor Mr Lake and his
daughter Rose used to lay claim to—the "rank of their own" which they
possessed as artists—was a pretension much more disagreeable to the

enrichment.interest_rationale: Sharp analysis of class resentment: working-class shopkeepers resent the Lakes' artistic pretensions more than gentry do.
enrichment.summary: The Lakes' claim to special artistic rank is more offensive to shopkeepers than to society proper, revealing class anxiety among the petit bourgeoisie.

text:
Thus in every sense Mr Cavendish
had done the very worst for himself by his ill-timed indulgence; and his
guilt was about the same with most of his critics whether he meant
perfectly well and innocently, or entertained the most guilty intentions
ever conceived by man.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Summary assertion that Cavendish's Saturday visit has damaged him equally whether innocent or guilty; reveals the arbitrary nature of social judgment.
enrichment.best_quote: his guilt was about the same with most of his critics whether he meant perfectly well and innocently, or entertained the most guilty intentions ever conceived by man.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish's ill-timed Saturday indulgence has wounded him fatally; society judges him equally guilty regardless of his actual intentions.

text:
And all his misfortunes were increased by the fact that the intervening
day was a Sunday.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reiteration that Sunday's timing compounds Cavendish's troubles; plot mechanism.
enrichment.summary: All Cavendish's misfortunes are magnified by the fact that Sunday falls between his visit and the election.

text:
Barbara Lake herself, who did not know what people
were saying, and who, if she had known, would not have cared, came to
church, as was natural, in the morning; and under pretence that the
family pew was full, had the assurance, as people remarked, to come to
the middle aisle, in that same silk dress which rustled like tin, and
made more demonstration than the richest draperies.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid portrait of Barbara attending church with provocative unconcern; establishes her character and social transgression.
enrichment.best_quote: under pretence that the family pew was full, had the assurance, as people remarked, to come to the middle aisle, in that same silk dress which rustled like tin
enrichment.summary: Barbara arrives at church in her conspicuous rustling silk dress, claiming the family pew is full, and sits in the middle aisle where all eyes scrutinize her.

text:
The pew-opener
disapproved of her as much as everybody else did, but she could not turn
the intruder out; and though Barbara had a long time to wait, and was
curiously inspected by all the eyes near her while she did so, the end
was that she got a seat in her rustling silk not very far from where
Lucilla sat in deep mourning, a model of every righteous observance.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Positioning of Barbara near Lucilla establishes a social contrast and tension.
enrichment.summary: The pew-opener cannot eject Barbara; she waits in her rustling dress and finally sits not far from Lucilla, who sits in deep mourning as a model of propriety.

text:
As
for poor Barbara, she too was very exemplary in church. She meant nobody
any harm, poor soul. She could not help the flashing of those big black
eyes, to which the level line above them gave such a curious appearance
of obliqueness—nor was it to be expected that she should deny herself
the use of her advantages, or omit to "take the second" in all the
canticles with such melodious liquid tones as made everybody stop and
look round.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Character study of Barbara: sympathetic portrait of her innocence and unconscious offence; demonstrates her natural charm and virtue.
enrichment.best_quote: She meant nobody any harm, poor soul. She could not help the flashing of those big black eyes, to which the level line above them gave such a curious appearance of obliqueness
enrichment.summary: Barbara sings beautifully in church with natural talent and good intention; she cannot help her striking eyes or melodious voice, yet both offend sensibilities.

text:
She had a perfect right to do it; indeed it was her duty, as
it is everybody's duty, to aid to the best of their ability in the
church-music of their parish, which was what Lucilla Marjoribanks
persisted in saying in answer to all objections. But the effect was
great in the congregation, and even the Rector himself was seen to
change colour as his eye fell upon the unlucky young woman.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shows Lucilla's principled defense of Barbara and the Rector's discomfort; demonstrates Lucilla's character and sets up the scandal's escalation.
enrichment.best_quote: it is everybody's duty, to aid to the best of their ability in the church-music of their parish
enrichment.summary: Lucilla defends Barbara's right to sing; the Rector visibly changes colour, unable to reconcile Barbara's beauty and voice with propriety.

text:
Mr
Cavendish, for his part, knew her voice the moment he heard it, and gave
a little start, and received such a look from his sister, who was
standing by him, as turned him to stone. Mrs Woodburn looked at him, and
so did her husband, and Mr Centum turned a solemnly inquiring
reproachful gaze upon him from the other side of the aisle.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dramatic moment: Cavendish recognizes Barbara's voice, his sister's reproachful look, and others' silent judgment converge; peak social embarrassment.
enrichment.best_quote: received such a look from his sister, who was standing by him, as turned him to stone
enrichment.summary: Cavendish recognizes Barbara's voice and reacts with a start; his sister Mrs Woodburn gives him a withering look; Mr Centum silently condemns him with a glance.

text:
"Oh, Harry,
you will kill me with vexation! why, for goodness' sake, did you let her
come?" his sister whispered when they had all sat down again. "Good
heavens! how could I help it?" cried poor Mr Cavendish, almost loud
enough to be heard.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dialogue showing Mrs Woodburn's dismay and Cavendish's helpless protest; intimate portrayal of sibling tension and political consequence.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh, Harry, you will kill me with vexation! why, for goodness' sake, did you let her come?
enrichment.summary: Mrs Woodburn whispers angrily, asking why Cavendish allowed Barbara to attend; he protests helplessly that he could not prevent her.

text:
And then by the slight, almost imperceptible, hum
around him, he felt that not only his sister and his committee, but the
Rector and all Carlingford, had their eyes upon him, and was thankful to
look up the lesson, poor man, and bury his face in it. It was a hard
punishment for the indiscretion of an hour.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Cavendish's public humiliation reaches its apex in church; he buries himself in the lesson while all eyes watch; vivid depiction of social torture.
enrichment.best_quote: It was a hard punishment for the indiscretion of an hour.
enrichment.summary: Cavendish feels the congregation's eyes upon him and takes refuge in the lesson; the narrator notes this severe punishment for a momentary indiscretion.

text:
But perhaps of all the people concerned it was the Rector who was the
most to be pitied.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition focusing sympathy on the Rector, who faces his own moral crisis from having endorsed Cavendish's repentance.
enrichment.summary: The Rector emerges as the most pitiable figure, having staked his honour on Cavendish's repentance.

text:
He had staked his honour upon Mr Cavendish's
repentance, and here was he going back, publicly to wallow in the
mire—and it was Sunday when such a worldly subject ought not to be
permitted to enter a good man's mind, much less to be discussed and
acted upon as it ought to be if anything was to be done; for there was
little more than this sacred day remaining in which to undo the mischief
which a too great confidence in human nature had wrought.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rich thematic content: the Rector's dilemma between Sunday's sacredness and the need for urgent action; his misplaced confidence in human nature.
enrichment.best_quote: here was he going back, publicly to wallow in the mire—and it was Sunday when such a worldly subject ought not to be permitted to enter a good man's mind
enrichment.summary: The Rector witnesses Cavendish's apparent backsliding just as Sunday prevents proper remedial action; his confidence in human nature proves false.

text:
And then, to
tell the truth, the Rector did not know how to turn back.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Exposition: the Rector's paralysis; he cannot reverse course without public embarrassment.
enrichment.summary: The Rector cannot openly retract his support without losing credibility.

text:
It would have
been hard, very hard, to have told all the people who confided in him
that he had never had any stronger evidence for Mr Cavendish's
repentance than he now had for his backsliding; and to give in, and let
the other side have it all their own way, and throw over the candidate
with whom he had identified himself, was as painful to Mr Bury as if,
instead of being very Low-Church, he had been the most muscular of
Christians.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Thematic exploration of institutional and personal integrity; the Rector's dilemma mirrors institutional contradictions.
enrichment.summary: The Rector cannot tell people he had no stronger evidence for Cavendish's repentance than for his backsliding; he must either cling to Cavendish or lose all credibility.

text:
Being in this state of mind, it may be supposed that his
sister's mild wonder and trembling speculations at lunch, when they were
alone together, were well qualified to raise some sparks of that old
Adam, who, though well kept under, still existed in the Rector's, as in
most other human breasts.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Character study: the Rector's moral struggle manifests in irritation at his sister's gentle questioning; human nature overtakes piety.
enrichment.summary: The Rector's sister's mild speculation at lunch provokes some of his old Adam; his piety is strained by stress.

text:
"But, dear Edward, I would not quite condemn him," Miss Bury said. "He
has been the cause of a good deal of remark, you know, and the poor girl
has been talked about. He may think it is his duty to make her amends.
For anything we can tell, he may have the most honourable
intentions——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dialogue: Miss Bury offers a charitable interpretation of Cavendish's motives; her gentle voice contrasts with the Rector's coming outburst.
enrichment.summary: Miss Bury suggests Cavendish may have honourable intentions in seeking Barbara to make her amends for the talk she has endured.

text:
"Oh, bother his honourable intentions!" said the Rector. Such an
exclamation from him was as bad as the most dreadful oath from an
ordinary man, and very nearly made Miss Bury drop from her chair in
amazement. Things must have gone very far indeed when the Rector himself
disregarded all proprieties and the sacredness of the day in such a
wildly-daring fashion.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Explosive moment: the Rector's profane outburst; his self-control shatters, revealing his authentic moral crisis beneath pious composure.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh, bother his honourable intentions!
enrichment.summary: The Rector exclaims 'Oh, bother his honourable intentions!' with such vehemence that Miss Bury is shocked; his composure fails him.

text:
For, to tell the truth, in his secret heart Mr
Bury was himself a little of the way of thinking of the people in Grove
Street.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Psychological insight: the Rector's secret agreement with popular class prejudice; authorial irony about clerical hypocrisy.
enrichment.best_quote: in his secret heart Mr Bury was himself a little of the way of thinking of the people in Grove Street.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reveals the Rector shares the class prejudice of Grove Street against Barbara Lake, despite his professed charity.

text:
Strictly speaking, if a man has done anything to make a young
woman be talked about, every well-principled person ought to desire that
he should make her amends; but at the same time, at such a crisis there
was little consolation in the fact that the candidate one was supporting
and doing daily battle for had honourable intentions in respect to
Barbara Lake.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Thematic exploration: moral principle vs. practical politics; Cavendish's honourable intentions are worse than useless to his candidacy.
enrichment.summary: The Rector recognizes that though principle demands Cavendish atone for Barbara's damaged reputation, his honourable intentions harm his election chances.

text:
If it had been Rose Lake, it would still have been a blow;
but Rose was unspeakably respectable, and nobody could have said a
syllable on the subject: while Barbara, who came to church in a tin
gown, and rustled up the middle aisle in it, attracting all eyes, and
took such a second in the canticles that she overwhelmed the choir
itself—Barbara, who had made people talk at Lucilla's parties, and had
been ten years away, wandering over the face of the earth, nobody could
tell where—governessing, singing, play-acting, perhaps, for anything
that anybody could tell!

enrichment.interest_rationale: Sharp character analysis: Barbara's behaviour and history invite class-based prejudice; Rose would be respectable, but Barbara's ten years abroad invite gossip.
enrichment.best_quote: Barbara, who had made people talk at Lucilla's parties, and had been ten years away, wandering over the face of the earth, nobody could tell where—governessing, singing, play-acting, perhaps, for anything that anybody could tell!
enrichment.summary: Rose would be acceptable as Cavendish's wife, being respectable and an artist of standing; Barbara's ten years of unexplained absence breed speculation about her morality.

text:
A clergyman, it is true, dared not have said
such a thing, and Mr Bury's remorse would have been bitter could he have
really believed himself capable even of thinking it; but still it is
certain that the unconscious, unexpressed idea in his mind was, that the
honourable intentions were the worst of it—that a candidate might be a
fool, or even an unrepentant sinner, and after all it would be chiefly
his own concern; but that so much as to dream of making Barbara Lake the
Member's wife, was the deepest insult that could be offered to
Carlingford.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Profound insight into the Rector's unconscious class hypocrisy; authorial irony reveals that marrying Barbara would be a worse insult to Carlingford than any sin.
enrichment.best_quote: that a candidate might be a fool, or even an unrepentant sinner, and after all it would be chiefly his own concern; but that so much as to dream of making Barbara Lake the Member's wife, was the deepest insult that could be offered to Carlingford.
enrichment.summary: The Rector admits to himself that Carlingford would forgive Cavendish any moral failing except marrying Barbara Lake—class prejudice trumps moral principle.

text:
The Rector carried his burden silently all day, and
scarcely opened his lips, as all his sympathetic following remarked; but
before he went to bed he made a singular statement, the complete
accuracy of which an impartial observer might be disposed to doubt, but
which Mr Bury uttered with profound sincerity, and with a sigh of
self-compassion.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrative transition: the Rector carries his burden silently, preparing for his later philosophical insight about Lucilla.
enrichment.summary: The Rector silently suffers through the day and prepares to make a singular remark before retiring.

text:
" Now  I understand Lucilla Marjoribanks," was what the
good man said, and he all but puffed out the candle he had just lighted,
with that sigh.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Unmissable highlight: the Rector's profound epiphany about Lucilla Marjoribanks; a singular moment of recognition that reframes the novel's social dynamics.
enrichment.best_quote: Now I understand Lucilla Marjoribanks
enrichment.summary: The Rector utters the line 'Now I understand Lucilla Marjoribanks' with profound sincerity and self-compassion, recognising her true power and influence.

text:
Lucilla, however, in her own person took no part in it at all, one way
or other. She shook hands very kindly with Barbara, and hoped she would
come and see her, and made it clearly apparent that  she  at least bore
no malice. "I am very glad I told Thomas to say nothing about it," she
said to Aunt Jemima, who, however, did not know the circumstances, and
was very little the wiser, as may be supposed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Shows Lucilla's magnanimity and emotional restraint; she maintains appearances and control while privately managing events.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla shakes Barbara's hand kindly, invites her to visit, and assures Aunt Jemima she told Thomas (the servant) not to gossip about the affair.

text:
And then the two ladies walked home together, and Miss Marjoribanks
devoted herself to her good books. It was almost the first moment of
repose that Lucilla had ever had in her busy life, and it was a repose
not only permitted but enjoined.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Exposition: Lucilla's unusual rest and her response to social expectations.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla walks home with Aunt Jemima and devotes herself to good books; she experiences rare repose that society permits given her mourning.

text:
Society, which had all along expected
so much from her, expected now that she should not find herself able for
any exertion; and Miss Marjoribanks responded nobly, as she had always
done, to the requirements of society.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Character study: Lucilla's perfect self-regulation; she responds to society's expectations of her mourning and frailty with composure.
enrichment.summary: Society expects Lucilla to be unable to exert herself, and she nobly responds to these expectations despite being capable of much more.

text:
To a mind less perfectly
regulated, the fact that the election which had been so interesting to
her was now about, as may be said, to take place without her, would have

bore it was not one of the least remarkable phenomena of the present
crisis. But the fact was that this Sunday was on the whole an oppressive
day.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Thematic depth: the election's removal from Lucilla's control is a significant trial; Sunday becomes oppressive as it removes her agency.

text:
Mr Ashburton came in for a moment, it is true, between services;
but he himself, though generally so steady, was unsettled and agitated. He had been bearing the excitement well until this last almost
incredible accident occurred, which made it possible that he might not
only win, but win by a large majority.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr Ashburton's agitation contrasts with his earlier steadiness; the scandal improves his chances and excites him.
enrichment.summary: Mr Ashburton visits between services, trembling with excitement at the possibility of a large majority after Cavendish's scandal.

text:
"The Dissenters have all held out
till now, and would not pledge themselves," he said to Lucilla, actually
with a tremble in his voice; and then he told her about Mr Tufton's
sermon and the wickedness in high places, and the hand imbrued

text:

just like those Dissenters. What harm was there in going to see her? I
heard of it last night, but even for your interest I would never have
spread such mere gossip as that."

enrichment.summary: Lucilla says it is like the Dissenters to spread such gossip, and that she would never have spoken of it, even for Ashburton's election.

text:

him a great deal of harm all the same," and then once more he got
restless and abstracted. "I suppose it is of no use asking you if you

text:
Lucilla shook her head, and the movement was more expressive than words.
"I did not think you would," said Mr Ashburton; and then he took her
hand, and his looks too became full of meaning. "Then I must say adieu,"
he said—"adieu until it is all over. I shall not have a moment that I
can call my own—this will be an eventful week for me."

text:

a novice as to be afraid of the appearance he would have to make at the
nomination. He did not contradict her, but he pressed her hand with a
look which was equivalent to kissing it, though he was not romantic
enough to go quite that length.

text:

could not but wonder a little what he could mean by looking forward to
an eventful week. For her own part, she could not but feel that after so
much excitement things would feel rather flat for the rest of the week,
and that it was almost wrong to have an election on a Tuesday.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's speculation about Ashburton's hidden meaning; reveals her awareness of romantic possibility and her keen observation.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla wonders what Ashburton means by 'eventful week', speculating he may have a hidden candidateship or contest in mind.

text:
Could it
be that Mr Ashburton had some other contest or candidateship in store
for himself which he had not told her about? Such a thing was quite
possible; but what had Lucilla in her mourning to do with worldly
contingencies?

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine reflection about Lucilla's mourning and propriety.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reflects that she ought not speculate about worldly contingencies while in mourning.

text:
She went back to her seat in the corner of the sofa and
her book of sermons, and read fifty pages before tea-time; she knew how
much, because she had put a mark in her book when Mr Ashburton came in. Marks are very necessary things generally in sermon-books; and Lucilla
could not but feel pleased to think that since her visitor went away she
had got over so much ground.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine domestic detail: Lucilla reads sermon-books and marks her progress.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reads fifty pages of sermon-books before tea, pleased to have made such progress, marked by a bookmark.

text:
To compare Carlingford to a volcano that night (and indeed all the next
day, which was the day of nomination) would be a stale similitude; and
yet in some respects it was like a volcano. It was not the same kind of
excitement which arises in a town where politics run very high—if there
are any towns nowadays in such a state of unsophisticated nature.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Authorial commentary on Carlingford's political excitement; distances the town from routine corruption or high politics, establishing its idealism.
enrichment.summary: The narrator reflects that Carlingford's excitement resembles a volcano, but differs from towns where politics run high or corruption prevails.

text:
Neither was it a place where simple corruption could carry the day; for
the freemen of Wharfside were, after all, but a small portion of the
population. It was in reality a quite ideal sort of contest—a contest
for the best man, such as would have pleased the purest-minded
philosopher.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Authorial irony about Carlingford's idealism; it is a contest for the best man, not a mercenary one—a rare phenomenon.
enrichment.summary: Carlingford's election is genuinely idealistic, not driven by simple corruption; it is a contest for the man most fit to represent the town.

text:
It was the man most fit to represent Carlingford for whom
everybody was looking, not a man to be baited about parish-rates and
Reform Bills and the Irish Church;—a man who lived in, or near the
town, and "dealt regular" at all the best shops; a man who would not
disgrace his constituency by any unlawful or injudicious sort of
love-making—who would attend to the town's interests and subscribe to
its charities, and take the lead in a general way.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Articulation of Carlingford's values: a respectable, resident candidate who attends to business, supports charities, and avoids scandal.
enrichment.best_quote: a man who lived in, or near the town, and "dealt regular" at all the best shops; a man who would not disgrace his constituency by any unlawful or injudicious sort of love-making
enrichment.summary: Carlingford seeks a man of respectability, local ties, commercial relationships, and domestic propriety—essentially a man of the town.

text:
This was what
Carlingford was looking for, as Miss Marjoribanks, with that intuitive
rapidity which was characteristic of her genius, had at once remarked;
and when everybody went home from church and chapel, though it was
Sunday, the whole town thrilled and throbbed with this great question.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Attribution of Lucilla's insight to her intuitive genius; she recognises Carlingford's true ideal before the election tests it.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla's intuitive rapidity grasped what Carlingford truly sought in a candidate, and the whole town throbs with this question on Sunday.

text:
People might have found it possible to condone a sin or wink at a mere
backsliding; but there were few so bigoted in their faith as to believe
that the man who was capable of marrying Barbara Lake could ever be the
man for Carlingford; and thus it was that Mr Cavendish, who had been
flourishing like a green bay-tree, withered away, as it were, in a
moment, and the place that had known him knew him no more.

Tom is not just like other people; and whatever happens, Nancy, you are
an old dear, and it shall never make any difference between you and me."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's acknowledgment of Tom's troublesome nature combined with her commitment to Nancy shows her characteristic balancing of duty and loyalty.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla assures Nancy that having a gentleman in the house has advantages and promises their relationship will endure unchanged.

text:
When she had said these words, Lucilla gave her faithful servant a hug,
and sent her off to look after Tom Marjoribanks's meal; and then she
herself went half-way downstairs and picked up the cards that were still
scattered about the landing, and found with satisfaction that the
Doctor's old punch-bowl was not broken.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's hug and tender action toward Nancy, combined with her practical check on the punch bowl, show her restored composure and affectionate authority.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla affectionately embraces Nancy and sends her off, then picks up the scattered cards and checks that her father's punch bowl is unbroken.

text:
All Tom's things were lying
below in the hall—heaps of queer Indian-looking baggage—tossed down
anyhow in a corner, as if the owner had been in much too great a hurry
to think of any secondary circumstances. "And it was there he met poor
Mr Ashburton," said Lucilla to herself, with a certain pathos. There it
was indeed that the encounter had taken place.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's contemplation of Tom's scattered baggage and recognition of where Mr Ashburton was encountered provides retrospective poignancy.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla observes Tom's hastily discarded baggage and identifies the spot where he encountered Mr Ashburton as they left.

text:
They had seen each other
but for a moment, but that moment had been enough to send the Member for
Carlingford away dejected, and to impress upon Tom's mind the
alternative that it was either to be "him or me." Miss Marjoribanks
contemplated the spot with a certain tender sentimental interest, as any
gentle moralist might look at a field of battle.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's romanticized contemplation of the brief encounter between Tom and Mr Ashburton, likening it to a field of battle, shows her poetic imagination.
enrichment.best_quote: Miss Marjoribanks contemplated the spot with a certain tender sentimental interest, as any gentle moralist might look at a field of battle.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla sentimentally contemplates the landing where Tom and Mr Ashburton met, viewing it as a crucial moment.

text:
What feelings must have
been in the minds of the two as they met and looked at each other! What
a dread sense of disappointment on the one side; what sharp stimulation
on the other! Thus Lucilla stood and looked down from her own landing
upon the scene of that encounter, full of pensive interest.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's empathetic reflection on the emotions of both men captures her restored composure and romantic imagination; the narrator's ironic tone complements her sentiment.
enrichment.best_quote: What feelings must have been in the minds of the two as they met and looked at each other!
enrichment.summary: Lucilla imagines the contrasting emotions the two men experienced upon encountering each other.

text:
And now it
was all over, and Mr Ashburton had passed away as completely as Mr
Chiltern, who was in his grave, poor man; or Mr Cavendish, who was going
to marry Barbara Lake. The thought of so sudden a revolution made
Lucilla giddy as she went thoughtfully upstairs. Poor Mr Ashburton! It
hardly seemed real even to Miss Marjoribanks when she sat down again in
the drawing-room, and confessed to herself that, after all, it was to be
Tom.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's giddiness and contemplative reassurance of herself that it is indeed 'to be Tom' shows her processing the extraordinary reversal and settling into her new reality.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reflects on the sudden revolution in her circumstances and how past suitors have been replaced by her engagement to Tom.

text:
But when he came downstairs again with his mother, Lucilla was quite
herself, and had got over all her weakness. Aunt Jemima, for her part,
was in a very agitated state of mind. Tom had come too soon or Mr
Ashburton too late, and all the fruits of her little bit of treachery
were accordingly lost, and at the same time, the treachery itself
remained, revealed at least to one person in the very clearest light.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's restoration of composure upon Aunt Jemima's arrival contrasts with her aunt's agitation; the narrative shift to Mrs John's anxiety provides new perspective.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla recovers completely; when Tom and his mother come downstairs, Aunt Jemima is very agitated about her interference being discovered.

text:
It did not seem possible to Aunt Jemima that Lucilla would not tell. If
she had not done it now, in the excitement of the moment, at least it
would come out some time when she was least expecting it, and her son's
esteem and confidence would be lost. Therefore it was with a very blank
countenance that Mrs John Marjoribanks came downstairs.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Jemima's anxiety about exposure of her 'treachery' reveals her vulnerable conscience and fear of her son's judgment.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Jemima fears that Lucilla will reveal her meddling in the match, which would damage her son's confidence in her.

text:
She dared not
say a word, and she had to kiss her niece, and take her to her maternal
bosom, Tom looking on all the while; but she gave Lucilla a look that
was pitiful to see. And when Tom finally was dismissed to his room, to
open his trunks, and show the things he had brought home, Aunt Jemima
drew near her future daughter with wistful guiltiness.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Jemima's constrained greetings and pitiful expression reveal her guilt without full revelation; her wistful interaction with Tom adds pathos.
enrichment.best_quote: she gave Lucilla a look that was pitiful to see
enrichment.summary: Aunt Jemima greets Lucilla with barely concealed distress while Tom watches; her guilt is evident in her expression.

text:
There was no
comfort to her in the thought of the India shawl, which her son had gone
to find. Any day, any hour, Lucilla might tell; and if the unlucky
mother were put on her defence, what could she say?

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition of Aunt Jemima's anxiety; the mention of the India shawl is a detail without substantial narrative weight.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Jemima dreads the moment when her interference might be revealed and worries about her son's esteem.

text:
"Lucilla," said the guilty woman, under her breath, "I am sure you think
it very strange. I don't attempt to deceive  you . I can't tell you how
thankful and glad I am that it has all ended so well; but you know,
Lucilla, in the first place, I did not know what your feelings were; and
I thought, perhaps, that if anything would tell, it would be a surprise,
and then——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Jemima's anxious confession reveals her duplicity; her attempt to justify her interference while seeking Lucilla's forgiveness shows her moral conflict.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Jemima anxiously confesses her lack of knowledge about Lucilla's feelings and suggests Mr Ashburton might have worked as a catalyst.

text:
"Did you, Aunt Jemima?" said Miss Marjoribanks, with gentle wonder. "I
thought you had been thinking of Mr Ashburton, for my part."

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's gentle, ironic response reveals her wisdom and forgiveness; her calm penetration of her aunt's attempted justification shows her psychological insight.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla gently confronts her aunt with the true motive for her meddling: concern for Mr Ashburton, not the catalyst theory.

text:
"And so I was, Lucilla," said the poor lady, with great relief and
eagerness. "I thought he was coming forward, and of course he would have
been a far better match than my Tom. I had to think for you both, my
dear. And then I never knew what your feelings were, nor if you would
care; and then it was not as if there had been a day fixed——"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Jemima's relief at being thus gently confronted and her continued justification reveal her character; her claim of uncertainty about fixed engagements is sophistic.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Jemima admits she was thinking of Mr Ashburton and worried about Lucilla's unspoken feelings, justifying her interference.

text:
"Dear Aunt Jemima," said Miss Marjoribanks, "if you are pleased now,
what does it matter? but I do hope you are pleased now?"

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's pragmatic forgiveness and gentle confirmation of her aunt's happiness show her magnanimity and continued management of emotional situations.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla accepts her aunt's justifications and asks whether she is satisfied with the outcome.

text:
And Mrs John took her niece into her arms again this time with better
will, and cried. "I am as happy as ever I can be," said the inconsistent
mother. "I always knew you were fond of each other, Lucilla; before you
knew it yourselves, I saw what would come of it. But my poor
brother-in-law——And you will make my boy happy, and never turn him
against his mother," cried the repentant sinner.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Aunt Jemima's emotional reconciliation and grateful relief are touching; her final plea about protecting Tom reveals her maternal anxiety and moral growth.
enrichment.summary: Aunt Jemima cries with joy, claims she always knew of Tom and Lucilla's affection, and begs Lucilla not to turn Tom against her.

text:
Lucilla was not the
woman to resist such an appeal. Mrs John had meant truly enough towards
her in other ways, if not in this way; and Miss Marjoribanks was fond of
her aunt, and it ended in a kiss of peace freely bestowed, and a vow of
protection and guidance from the strong to the weak, though the last was
only uttered in the protectress's liberal heart.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lucilla's generous response to her aunt's appeal shows her mature magnanimity; her vow of protection and guidance reveals the novel's ultimate thematic resolution.
enrichment.best_quote: and a vow of protection and guidance from the strong to the weak, though the last was only uttered in the protectress's liberal heart
enrichment.summary: Lucilla resists her aunt's appeal and responds with a kiss of peace; she silently vows to protect and guide her aunt.

text:
When Miss Marjoribanks had time to consider the prospect which had thus
so suddenly opened before her, it also had its difficulties, like
everything else in the world. Her marriage now could not be the
straightforward business it might have been had it been Mr Ashburton
instead of Tom.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the practical complications of Lucilla's engagement to Tom rather than Mr Ashburton, introducing the central tension of the chapter.
enrichment.summary: Lucilla reflects that marrying Tom presents more difficulties than marrying Mr Ashburton would have, as Tom has no profession or established position.
